units.title: OUTER RIM
units.theme: Identifying people and things, and anchoring a moment in time

overview.intro: Every long journey starts with names and coordinates. This sector gives you two ways of being precise: relative clauses, which tell your listener exactly which person or thing you mean, and it-clauses with “when”, which pin a feeling or a judgement to a moment. Both let you replace two thin sentences with one adult sentence.
goals: Use who and that as subjects and objects of defining relative clauses.
Decide when the relative pronoun can be omitted and when it must stay.
Build it-clauses with adverbial when to describe situations and reactions.
overview.outcome: By the end you can define any person, object or job in one sentence, and describe three situations that annoy, please or surprise you using it-clauses.

vocab.def: to irritate someone, usually by repeating something.
vocab.use: The thing that annoys is the subject: “It gets on my nerves when people talk loudly.”
examples: It gets on my nerves when someone interrupts me.
His constant tapping got on my nerves.
vocab.colloc: really get on my nerves · get on your nerves

vocab.def: that you can trust to work or to behave well.
vocab.use: For people, machines and sources: “a reliable colleague”, “a reliable source”. Opposite: unreliable.
examples: I need someone who is reliable.
The old laptop isn’t reliable any more.
vocab.colloc: highly reliable · a reliable source · reliable service

vocab.def: thinking about other people’s feelings.
vocab.use: “Considerate of / towards someone”. Not the same as “considerable”, which means large.
examples: She’s a considerate neighbour who never plays loud music.
It was considerate of you to call.
vocab.colloc: very considerate · considerate towards others

vocab.def: to tolerate something unpleasant without complaining.
vocab.use: Three parts, always together, always with an object: “I can’t put up with it.”
examples: I can’t put up with people who are always late.
She puts up with a lot at work.
vocab.colloc: put up with it · can’t put up with

vocab.def: a small thing that irritates you personally.
vocab.use: Countable, usually with a possessive: “my biggest pet peeve”. Informal.
examples: My pet peeve is people who don’t answer messages.
Loud chewing is her pet peeve.
vocab.colloc: my biggest pet peeve · a common pet peeve

vocab.def: to admire and respect someone.
vocab.use: Inseparable, three parts: “I look up to her.” Opposite: “look down on”.
examples: He’s someone I really look up to.
I look up to teachers who stay patient.
vocab.colloc: look up to a mentor · someone to look up to

vocab.def: deserving to be trusted.
vocab.use: For people and information: “a trustworthy witness”. Slightly more formal than “reliable”.
examples: A friend is someone who is trustworthy.
Is the website trustworthy?
vocab.colloc: completely trustworthy · a trustworthy source

vocab.def: to be very interested in something (informal).
vocab.use: “Be into + noun / -ing”: “I’m into astronomy.” Very common in spoken English.
examples: She’s really into old films.
I’m not into crowded places.
vocab.colloc: really into · not into it · what are you into

vocab.def: to annoy someone intensely.
vocab.use: “It drives me crazy when…” is the standard it-clause pattern.
examples: It drives me crazy when the lift is out of order.
That noise is driving me crazy.
vocab.colloc: drive me crazy · drive you mad

vocab.def: a person you work with.
vocab.use: Countable, neutral. “Workmate” is informal; “co-worker” is common in American English.
examples: I have a colleague who speaks four languages.
My colleagues are very supportive.
vocab.colloc: a former colleague · a close colleague

grammar.name: Relative pronouns as subjects and objects; pronoun omission
grammar.short: a person who listens · the film (that) we saw
grammar.rule: A defining relative clause identifies which person or thing you mean. “Who” refers to people, “that” refers to people and things, “which” refers to things. The pronoun can replace the subject or the object of its own clause — and only the object pronoun can be left out.
form: Subject pronoun (cannot be omitted): I like people who listen. / an app that works offline.
Object pronoun (can be omitted): the person (who/that) I met · the film (that) we saw.
Things: a phone which/that has a good camera.
Possession: the colleague whose laptop was stolen.
With a preposition at the end: the person (who) I spoke to.
notes: Never repeat the subject or object inside the clause: “the man who he called me” and “the book that I read it” are both wrong.
Test for omission: if a noun or pronoun follows the gap, the pronoun is an object and can be dropped — “the film I saw”.
A subject pronoun can never be dropped, because the clause would have no subject: “the man lives here” is a different sentence.
“Whom” is the formal object form for people and is normally replaced by “who” or nothing in speech.
In defining clauses there are no commas. Commas turn the clause into extra information, which you will meet in sector 14.
grammar.deep: Relative clauses are the fastest upgrade available at B1, because they let you say in one sentence what you previously said in two: “I have a colleague. She speaks four languages” becomes “I have a colleague who speaks four languages.” The whole mechanism reduces to a single question — what job is the relative pronoun doing inside its own clause? If it is the subject, it must stay, because English clauses cannot exist without a subject. If it is the object, the clause already has a subject, so the pronoun becomes optional and native speakers drop it constantly, which is why “the film I saw last night” sounds so much more natural than the fully marked version. The other habit to break is doubling: once the pronoun has replaced the object, nothing goes in the object slot, so “the book that I read it” contains one object too many.
examples: I admire people who admit their mistakes.
The app that I downloaded yesterday keeps crashing.
She’s the colleague I share an office with.
Anything that saves time is worth trying.
grammar.watch: Do not put an extra pronoun in the clause: “the song that I like it” must be “the song that I like”.
more: The colleague who trained me has just been promoted.
That’s the app that keeps logging me out.
She’s the only person I trust with the accounts.
Anything that saves a step is worth doing.
The report we submitted last week has been approved.
People who apologise quickly are easier to work with.

fix.wrong: the song that I like it
fix.right: the song that I like
fix.why: The relative pronoun already stands for the object; you cannot repeat it.

fix.wrong: The man which called left a message.
fix.right: The man who called left a message.
fix.why: “Which” never refers to people.

fix.wrong: The people work here are friendly.
fix.right: The people who work here are friendly.
fix.why: A subject pronoun cannot be omitted.

drill.name: Keep it or drop it
drill.prompt: Join each pair with a relative clause, then say whether the pronoun can be dropped and why.
items: I know an engineer. She fixes anything.
This is the file. You asked for it.
That’s the café. It closed last month.
Those are the students. I taught them last year.
Here’s the tool. It solved the problem.

dialogue.line: Who’s the person who signs these off?
The supervisor you met on Monday.
The one who gave the safety talk?
That’s her. Anything that touches the log needs her signature.

grammar.sound: When the object pronoun disappears, the two nouns run straight together: “the file you sent”. A pause in that gap sounds like hesitation, not grammar.

grammar.name: It-clauses and adverbial clauses with “when”
grammar.short: It bothers me when people are late.
grammar.rule: An it-clause puts a reaction or a judgement first and the situation second. The “it” is a placeholder; the real content arrives in the “when” clause, which describes the moment or the recurring situation that produces the reaction.
form: It + verb + object + when + clause → It annoys me when people cancel late.
It + be + adjective + when + clause → It’s frustrating when nobody replies.
It + be + noun + when + clause → It’s a problem when the system is down.
With “if” for a possible situation: It’s fine if you arrive late.
Reversed for emphasis: When people cancel late, it really annoys me.
notes: The verbs in this pattern are all reaction verbs: annoy, bother, upset, please, surprise, worry, irritate, drive me crazy.
“When” here means “every time that”, so the clause takes the present simple even though the reaction is general.
Do not use “will” in the when-clause: “It bothers me when he will arrive late” is wrong.
The adjective version needs no object: “It’s annoying when…”, not “It’s annoying me when…” unless you really mean right now.
The whole structure can be reversed, and the when-clause then takes a comma: “When people are late, it bothers me.”
grammar.deep: English likes to delay heavy information, and the it-clause is one of its main tools for doing so. Instead of making a long situation the subject — “People cancelling arrangements at the last minute annoys me” — the sentence opens with an empty “it”, delivers the reaction immediately, and only then explains the trigger. That order is easier to process, which is why spoken English uses it constantly for opinions and complaints. The “when” inside these clauses is not really about a single occasion: it means “every time that”, which is why the tense stays in the present simple even when you are describing something habitual and irritating. Learn the two variants together — “it + verb + object” for a personal reaction (“it bothers me”) and “it + be + adjective” for a general judgement (“it’s frustrating”) — and you can react to almost anything with precision.

chart.title: It-clause patterns
rows: It annoys me when people push in.
It’s rude when someone doesn’t reply.
It’s a nuisance when the wifi drops.
It’s fine if you need more time.
It surprises me that nobody noticed.
When people shout, it upsets me.

examples: It really bothers me when people talk during films.
It’s frustrating when you wait an hour and nobody comes.
It’s not a problem when you tell me in advance.
When my neighbours play music at midnight, it drives me crazy.
grammar.watch: Keep the when-clause in the present simple, and do not add an object to the adjective version: “It’s annoying when…”, not “It’s annoying me when…”.
more: It bothers me when people reply only to half the email.
It’s frustrating when the system logs you out mid-form.
It makes a difference when someone explains the reason.
It really annoys me when meetings start late.
It’s a relief when a difficult call is over.
It surprised everyone when she turned the offer down.

fix.wrong: It bothers me that people are late all the time.
fix.right: It bothers me when people are late.
fix.why: A recurring situation takes a when-clause; the that-clause names a single fact.

fix.wrong: Bothers me when people are late.
fix.right: It bothers me when people are late.
fix.why: English requires the placeholder “it” as subject.

fix.wrong: It’s annoying when someone will interrupt you.
fix.right: It’s annoying when someone interrupts you.
fix.why: A when-clause about general behaviour takes the present simple.

drill.name: Reaction first
drill.prompt: Turn each situation into an it-clause, then repeat it with a different reaction verb or adjective.
items: people cancel at the last minute

dialogue.line: What gets on your nerves at work?
It bothers me when people book a meeting with no agenda.
Fair. It annoys me when nobody speaks in them.
And it’s a relief when someone finally says what they actually want.

contrast.title: Which frame?
rows: What annoys me is the delay.

grammar.sound: The placeholder “it” is unstressed and almost swallowed; the stress lands on the reaction word: “it BOTHers me when…”.

speaking.text: Define ten jobs, objects or types of person without naming them, using only defining relative clauses. Your partner guesses each one.
Share five things that get on your nerves, each as an it-clause with “when”. Your partner responds with agreement or a counter-example.
Describe the four people you would take on a long mission, each with a relative clause explaining why: “someone who…”, “a person that…”.

tips: Ask what job the pronoun does in its own clause — subject stays, object can go.
Never leave an extra pronoun behind: “the film that I saw”, not “that I saw it”.
The when-clause of an it-clause stays in the present simple.

quiz.q: That’s the engineer ___ fixed the navigation system.
quiz.explain: “Who” is the subject of the relative clause, so it must stay and cannot be followed by another subject.

dynamics.name: Define your classmate
dynamics.how: Each student writes three defining relative clauses about people in the room without naming them. Cards are shuffled and read out; the class identifies the person and challenges any clause that could describe two people.
dynamics.payoff: Ambiguity is punished, so the clauses become genuinely defining.

dynamics.name: Pet peeve ladder
dynamics.how: Groups collect eight it-clause complaints and rank them from mild to unbearable. Every placement must be argued with a full it-clause, and the group must agree on the top three.
dynamics.payoff: Negotiation produces dozens of the target frame instead of a list.

dynamics.name: Drop the pronoun
dynamics.how: Student A reads a sentence with a relative pronoun; B must say it again dropping the pronoun if possible, or say “subject — it stays”. Ten each, then swap.
dynamics.payoff: Trains the one decision learners actually get wrong.

dynamics.name: Twenty questions, defined
dynamics.how: One student thinks of an object; the class narrows it down with relative clauses only: “Is it something that you use at work?”
dynamics.payoff: Forces the structure into question form, which the textbook rarely does.

writing.title: The people I work with
writing.brief: Describe three people you work or study with, identifying each one with a defining relative clause rather than a name. Finish with a paragraph of it-clauses about what you appreciate and what irritates you in a colleague.
criteria: Four defining relative clauses, at least one with the pronoun dropped.
Four it-clauses with when, at least two using different reaction verbs.
No repeated object pronoun inside a clause.

homework.title: Ten definitions, five reactions
homework.task: Write ten sentences defining objects, places or people with relative clauses, marking which pronouns could be dropped. Then write five it-clauses about situations from your week.

test.q: That’s the engineer ___ fixed the navigation system.
test.explain: “Who” is the subject of the clause and cannot be dropped or doubled.

test.q: This is the report ___ .
options: that I told you about it
test.explain: The object pronoun can be dropped, but the object cannot be repeated.

test.q: ___ me when people reply to half the question.
test.explain: The frame needs the placeholder “it”.

test.q: It’s frustrating when the system ___ you out.
test.explain: A general when-clause takes the present simple.

test.q: Anything ___ saves time is worth trying.
test.explain: “That” follows anything, everything, nothing and something.

Under them, one sentence written twice — once with the pronoun, once without — with an arrow marked OBJECT ONLY.
A red box: “the song that I like it” with “it” crossed out.
Lower half: IT + verb / be + adjective / be + noun, each with an empty WHEN slot to fill from the class.

units.title: CARGO BAY
units.theme: Naming activities, and measuring one thing against another

overview.intro: Two skills for building arguments. First, gerund phrases, which turn a whole activity into a noun so it can be the subject or object of a sentence. Second, the full comparison system: not only adjectives, but nouns, verbs and past participles, so you can compare quantities, actions and states with equal precision.
goals: Use gerund phrases as subjects and objects of sentences.
Compare with adjectives, nouns, verbs and past participles.
Choose between as … as, more … than and not as … as accurately.
overview.outcome: By the end you can argue for one option over another in six sentences, each using a different comparison structure.

vocab.def: to stop doing something, usually a habit.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or -ing: “give up smoking”. Separable with a pronoun: “give it up”.
examples: Giving up sugar was harder than I expected.
She gave up trying to fix it.
vocab.colloc: give up smoking · never give up · give it up

vocab.def: worth the time, money or effort involved.
vocab.use: Before a noun (“a worthwhile investment”) or after “be” (“it was worthwhile”).
examples: Learning a second language is worthwhile.
It was a worthwhile detour.
vocab.colloc: a worthwhile experience · well worthwhile

vocab.def: to advance towards a goal.
vocab.use: “Progress” is uncountable: “make good progress”, never “progresses”. Never “do progress”.
examples: Practising every day is the only way to make progress.
We’ve made a lot of progress.
vocab.colloc: make good progress · slow progress

vocab.def: taking a lot of time.
vocab.use: Hyphenated before a noun: “a time-consuming process”. Also after “be”.
examples: Commuting by bus is time-consuming.
The paperwork was extremely time-consuming.
vocab.colloc: a time-consuming task · less time-consuming

vocab.def: good enough to justify the cost or effort.
vocab.use: “It’s worth + -ing” or “worth it”. Never an infinitive: not “worth to try”.
examples: The course was expensive, but it was worth it.
It’s worth checking the price first.
vocab.colloc: well worth it · not worth the trouble

vocab.def: a good point / a disadvantage.
vocab.use: “The advantage of + -ing”, “the main drawback is that…”. Both countable.
examples: The advantage of flying is speed.
The only drawback is the price.
vocab.colloc: a big advantage · the main drawback

vocab.def: to start a new activity or hobby; to occupy space or time.
vocab.use: Separable: “take up running”, “it takes up too much space”.
examples: I took up swimming last year.
That sofa takes up half the room.
vocab.colloc: take up a hobby · take up space · take up time

vocab.def: working well without wasting time or resources.
vocab.use: For systems, machines and people: “an efficient process”. Adverb: efficiently.
examples: Cycling is more efficient than driving in the centre.
She’s an extremely efficient organiser.
vocab.colloc: highly efficient · fuel-efficient · work efficiently

vocab.term: to be similar to / different from
vocab.def: comparing likeness and difference.
vocab.use: Fixed prepositions: “similar to”, “different from” (also “to” in British English). Never “different than” in careful writing.
examples: This model is similar to the older one.
Life here is very different from what I expected.
vocab.colloc: remarkably similar to · slightly different from

vocab.def: not nearly; far from.
vocab.use: Used to strengthen a negative comparison: “nowhere near as expensive as”.
examples: It’s nowhere near as difficult as it looks.
We’re nowhere near finished.
vocab.colloc: nowhere near as good as · nowhere near enough

vocab.def: by a very large margin.
vocab.use: Strengthens a comparative or a superlative: “by far the cheapest”, “far more reliable”.
examples: This is by far the most reliable option.
She’s by far the fastest reader on the team.
vocab.colloc: by far the best · by far the cheapest · not by far

grammar.name: Gerund phrases as subjects and objects
grammar.short: Learning a language takes patience.
grammar.rule: A gerund is the -ing form used as a noun. A gerund phrase — the gerund plus its own objects and modifiers — behaves as a single noun, so it can be the subject of a sentence, the object of a verb, or the object of a preposition. As a subject it always takes a singular verb.
form: Subject: Learning two languages at once is demanding.
Object of a verb: I enjoy working in the evenings.
Object of a preposition: She’s good at solving problems.
Negative gerund: Not answering was a mistake.
After certain verbs only: avoid, enjoy, finish, keep, mind, suggest, recommend, consider.
notes: A gerund subject is always singular, however long the phrase: “Reading long technical reports is tiring.”
Every preposition takes a gerund, never an infinitive: “interested in learning”, “instead of waiting”, “before leaving”.
Verbs of aiming take infinitives instead: want, hope, plan, decide, learn, try → “I hope to travel”.
The negative goes before the gerund: “not knowing the answer”, never “knowing not”.
The alternative “it + infinitive” pattern says almost the same thing: “Learning is useful” / “It’s useful to learn.”
grammar.deep: The gerund exists so that an action can occupy a noun’s position in a sentence. That is why it is the natural subject for generalisations: “Arriving late creates a bad impression” talks about the activity itself, not about any particular arrival. Two consequences follow. The gerund phrase behaves as one unit, so the verb agrees with the whole phrase in the singular no matter how many nouns appear inside it — a rule that catches learners out in sentences like “Managing three projects at once is exhausting”. And because prepositions require noun-like objects, every preposition is automatically followed by a gerund, which is why “I’m thinking about changing jobs” cannot become “to change”. The competing pattern, “it + adjective + infinitive”, expresses the same idea with the judgement in front; alternating between the two is what keeps a paragraph of opinions from sounding mechanical.

chart.title: Where gerund phrases go
rows: It saves time to work from home.

examples: Studying two hours a day is more effective than studying ten hours once a week.
I don’t mind working late, but I hate starting early.
She succeeded in persuading the whole team.
Not knowing the language made everything slower.
grammar.watch: A gerund subject takes a singular verb, and every preposition takes -ing: “good at solving”, never “good at to solve”.
more: Learning two languages at once is demanding but possible.
Skipping the checklist is what caused the fault.
She’s good at explaining complicated things simply.
Not answering the email was a mistake.
We saved a week by automating the report.
I don’t mind working late; what I hate is starting early.

fix.wrong: To learn a language take time.
fix.right: Learning a language takes time.
fix.why: A gerund subject is singular, and the gerund is the natural subject form here.

fix.wrong: She’s good at to solve problems.
fix.right: She’s good at solving problems.
fix.why: Every preposition is followed by -ing, never by an infinitive.

fix.wrong: Don’t answering the email was a mistake.
fix.right: Not answering the email was a mistake.
fix.why: A gerund is negated with “not” placed directly before it.

drill.name: Turn it into a subject
drill.prompt: Convert each activity into a gerund phrase and use it as the subject of a sentence with a singular verb.

dialogue.line: Is the certification worth it?
Studying for it takes about six months.
And after that?
Having it opens doors. Not having it doesn’t close them, but it slows things down.

grammar.sound: A gerund subject carries the main stress on its own content word, and the verb that follows is short and unstressed: “LEARNing a language TAKES time.”

grammar.name: Comparisons with adjectives, nouns, verbs and past participles
grammar.short: cheaper than · as much space as · works harder than · better organised than
grammar.rule: English compares four different kinds of word, and the structure changes for each. Adjectives take -er or “more”; nouns take “more / fewer / less” and “as much / many … as”; verbs take “more / less” after the verb; past participles take “more / better / worse” before them.
form: Adjectives: cheaper than · more expensive than · as clean as · not as modern as.
Nouns (countable): more options than · fewer delays than · as many rooms as.
Nouns (uncountable): more space than · less noise than · as much light as.
Verbs: She works harder than I do. / I travel less than I used to.
Past participles: better organised than · more crowded than · worse designed than.
notes: “Fewer” goes with countable nouns and “less” with uncountable ones: fewer people, less traffic.
With verbs the comparison word follows the verb: “He complains more than anyone”, not “He more complains”.
Past participles used as adjectives keep “more / better / worse” in front: “more relaxed”, “better paid”, never “relaxeder”.
Strengthen a comparison with much, far, a lot, slightly, a bit or nowhere near: “far more expensive”, “nowhere near as fast”.
Keep the two things comparable: “My flat is smaller than yours”, not “than you”.
grammar.deep: Most learners can compare adjectives and stop there, which limits what they can argue. The system is wider: any word class can be compared, and the structure follows the class rather than the meaning. Notice that quantity comparisons split by countability, exactly as quantifiers do, so “fewer delays” and “less noise” are not interchangeable stylistic choices but grammatical requirements. Verbs are compared after the verb, which feels unnatural at first because the comparison word arrives late: “this model consumes less than the old one”. And past participles behave as adjectives that have already been formed from verbs, so they cannot take -er and must take “more”, “better” or “worse” instead. Once you can move between all four, a single argument can compare cost (adjective), features (countable noun), space (uncountable noun), performance (verb) and build quality (participle) without repeating a structure.
examples: The new terminal has more gates but fewer shops than the old one.
This engine uses less fuel and runs more quietly than the previous model.
She practises more than anyone else in the group.
The second proposal was better presented, though it was nowhere near as detailed.
grammar.watch: “Fewer” with countable nouns, “less” with uncountable ones, and “more” before a past participle: “more relaxed”, never “relaxeder”.
more: This model is cheaper and considerably more reliable than the last one.
It has fewer moving parts and uses less energy.
She works harder than anyone else on the shift.
The second version is far better organised than the first.
There isn’t nearly as much storage as we were promised.
Nothing is as frustrating as a queue that doesn’t move.

fix.wrong: less delays
fix.right: fewer delays
fix.why: “Delays” is countable, so it takes “fewer”.

fix.wrong: more cheaper
fix.right: cheaper
fix.why: Never use “more” with a comparative ending in -er.

fix.wrong: It works more hard than the old one.
fix.right: It works harder than the old one.
fix.why: Short adverbs form the comparative with -er, like the adjective.

drill.name: Four ways to compare
drill.prompt: Compare the two things four times: with an adjective, a countable noun, an uncountable noun and a verb.

dialogue.line: Is the new model actually better?
It has fewer parts and it uses less power.
Is it faster, though?
Not by far. It just runs more quietly and breaks down less often.

grammar.sound: “Than” is reduced to /ðən/ and links onto the word before it: “cheaper than” becomes /ˈtʃiːpəðən/. Stressing “than” makes the comparison sound argumentative.

speaking.text: Compare two ways of doing something — commuting, studying, cooking — using one comparison of each type: adjective, countable noun, uncountable noun, verb and past participle.
Make eight generalisations that begin with a gerund phrase. Your partner must agree or disagree and give a reason.
Sell your city, your job or your favourite app to the group. Every claim must be a comparison, and you may not repeat a structure.

tips: Gerund subjects are singular, however long the phrase.
Every preposition takes -ing — no exceptions.
Countable takes fewer, uncountable takes less.

quiz.q: This model has ___ moving parts and uses ___ energy than the old one.
quiz.explain: “Parts” is countable, so it takes “fewer”; “energy” is uncountable, so it takes “less”.

dynamics.name: Product face-off
dynamics.how: Each pair receives two competing products with spec sheets and must produce eight comparisons, one from each row of the contrast table, then recommend one.
dynamics.payoff: The table becomes a checklist, so the rare types get produced too.

dynamics.name: Gerund headlines
dynamics.how: Groups write six headlines that all begin with a gerund phrase (“Working from home saves…”), then defend the claim in one sentence each.
dynamics.payoff: Headlines force the gerund into subject position naturally.

dynamics.name: Fewer or less
dynamics.how: Teacher calls out nouns; students respond with FEWER or LESS and one full sentence. Any hesitation passes the turn.
dynamics.payoff: Isolates the countability error at speed.

dynamics.name: Ranking auction
dynamics.how: Groups rank six options (jobs, cities, apps) and must justify each position with a comparative and an “as … as” sentence. Other groups may challenge any unsupported claim.
dynamics.payoff: Equality structures appear, which comparatives alone never force.

writing.title: Two options, one recommendation
writing.brief: Compare two real options you have considered — two courses, two phones, two routes. Use at least six comparisons covering adjectives, nouns and verbs, and open the piece with a gerund phrase as the subject.
criteria: Two gerund phrases in subject position with singular verbs.
Six comparisons, including one “as … as” and one with fewer or less.
No double comparatives.

homework.title: Compare and justify
homework.task: Write eight comparative sentences about things in your daily life, one from each row of the contrast table, then rewrite three of them as equality sentences with “as … as”.

test.q: ___ two languages at once is demanding.
test.explain: A gerund phrase is the natural subject form.

test.q: This model has ___ moving parts and uses ___ energy.
test.explain: Parts are countable, energy is not.

test.q: She’s very good at ___ problems.
test.explain: A preposition is always followed by -ing.

test.q: He works ___ than anyone on the team.
test.explain: Short adverbs take -er, and never with “more”.

test.q: There isn’t ___ storage as we expected.
test.explain: “Storage” is uncountable, so it takes “as much … as”.

units.title: DOCKING RING
units.theme: Asking for things without demanding them

overview.intro: A docking manoeuvre is all negotiation. This sector covers the whole request system — modals, if-clauses and gerunds — and then the indirect forms that let you ask a stranger, an official or a superior for something without sounding like you are giving orders.
goals: Make requests with can, could, would and Would you mind + -ing.
Use if-clauses to ask permission politely: Do you mind if I…?
Convert direct questions into indirect requests and questions with correct word order.
overview.outcome: By the end you can ask for six favours at three levels of politeness and get information from a stranger using only indirect questions.

vocab.def: a helpful action you do because someone asks.
vocab.use: “Do someone a favour”, “ask a favour”. The opener “Can you do me a favour?” prepares your listener.
examples: Can you do me a favour and check this?
She asked me for a favour.
vocab.colloc: do me a favour · a big favour · return the favour

vocab.def: to be bothered or annoyed by something.
vocab.use: “Would you mind + -ing” is a request; “I don’t mind” means it is fine. Answering “yes” to “Would you mind…?” is a refusal.
examples: Would you mind waiting outside?
I don’t mind at all.
vocab.colloc: would you mind · never mind · I don’t mind

vocab.def: a softener before bad news or a refusal.
vocab.use: Nothing to do with fear: “I’m afraid I can’t” is the standard polite “no”.
examples: I’m afraid I can’t help you today.
I’m afraid the office is closed.
vocab.colloc: I’m afraid not · I’m afraid so

vocab.def: to want to know something.
vocab.use: The classic indirect opener: “I wonder where he lives.” Never invert after it.
examples: I was wondering if you could help me.
I wonder why she left so early.
vocab.colloc: I wonder if · I was wondering whether

vocab.def: the more formal alternative to “if” inside a reported question.
vocab.use: Use it when there are two options, and always after a preposition: “it depends on whether…”.
examples: Could you tell me whether the shop is open?
I’m not sure whether he got my message.
vocab.colloc: whether or not · it depends on whether

vocab.def: to pause because you are unsure.
vocab.use: “Hesitate to + verb”: “Don’t hesitate to ask.” A standard polite closing in emails.
examples: Don’t hesitate to contact me.
She hesitated before answering.
vocab.colloc: don’t hesitate to ask · hesitate for a moment

vocab.def: to be too busy to do something.
vocab.use: Usually with “be”: “I’m tied up until four.” A polite way of declining.
examples: I’m afraid I’m tied up all morning.
He was tied up in a meeting.
vocab.colloc: tied up in a meeting · tied up all day

vocab.def: to help someone.
vocab.use: “Give me a hand with + noun / -ing”: “give me a hand carrying this”.
examples: Could you give me a hand with these boxes?
She gave us a hand for an hour.
vocab.colloc: give me a hand with · need a hand

vocab.def: immediately.
vocab.use: A natural way to accept a request: “I’ll do it right away.” Synonym: straight away.
examples: I’ll send it right away.
He answered right away.
vocab.colloc: right away · straight away

vocab.def: to be grateful for something.
vocab.use: “I’d appreciate it if you could…” is a very polite request. Note the obligatory “it”.
examples: I’d appreciate it if you could reply today.
I really appreciate your help.
vocab.colloc: I’d appreciate it if · greatly appreciate

vocab.def: used to make a question sound tentative and less demanding.
vocab.use: Slots into the middle or end of a question: “Do you know, by any chance, where the office is?”
examples: Are you going that way by any chance?
Would you have a pen by any chance?
vocab.colloc: by any chance · do you by any chance know

grammar.name: Requests with modals, if-clauses and gerunds
grammar.short: Could you help? Do you mind if I sit here? Would you mind waiting?
grammar.rule: English grades politeness in requests by distance from reality. “Can” is direct, “could” and “would” are hypothetical and therefore politer, and “Would you mind + -ing” is the most indirect because it asks about the other person’s feelings rather than their actions.
form: Modal + base verb: Can / Could / Will / Would you open the window?
Permission for yourself: Can I / Could I / May I use your phone?
If-clause permission: Do you mind if I sit here? / Would you mind if I opened the window?
Gerund request: Would you mind opening the window?
Very polite: I’d appreciate it if you could send it today.
notes: “Would you mind” takes -ing, never an infinitive: “Would you mind waiting?”
The answers to “Would you mind…?” are inverted: “No, not at all” means yes, I will. Most speakers reply “Sure” or “Of course” to avoid the confusion.
“Do you mind if I…” takes a present tense; “Would you mind if I…” takes a past form: “if I borrowed your charger”.
Longer requests are politer: adding “possibly”, “just” or a reason increases courtesy.
When you refuse, give a reason — in English a bare “no” is heard as a rebuke.
grammar.deep: Politeness in English is not a vocabulary list but a strategy of leaving the other person an exit, and every step up the scale widens that exit. A bare imperative gives none. “Can you…?” asks about ability, which is theoretically refusable. “Could you…?” moves into the hypothetical, so the request is one step removed from reality. “Would you mind…?” does not ask about the action at all — it asks whether the action would bother you, which is exactly why the polarity of the answer flips. Learners lose ground in two opposite directions: some stay at the direct end and sound demanding, others use maximum politeness with close colleagues and sound cold or sarcastic. Match the level to the size of the favour and the closeness of the relationship, and remember that adding a reason does more for your tone than any extra modal.

chart.title: Politeness scale for requests
rows: Do you mind if I open it?
when you are the one acting
I’d appreciate it if you could…

examples: Could you possibly send me the file before five?
Do you mind if I join you? — Not at all.
Would you mind giving me a hand with these boxes?
I’d appreciate it if you could confirm by Friday.
grammar.watch: “Would you mind” + -ing, and remember that “No, not at all” is an acceptance, not a refusal.
more: Could you possibly send me the file before five?
Do you mind if I sit here? — Not at all, go ahead.
Would you mind waiting a couple of minutes?
I’d appreciate it if you could confirm in writing.
Can I borrow your charger for a second?
Would it be all right if I left ten minutes early?

fix.wrong: Would you mind to wait?
fix.right: Would you mind waiting?
fix.why: “Would you mind” is always followed by a gerund.

fix.wrong: Do you mind if I sat here?
fix.right: Do you mind if I sit here?
fix.why: “Do you mind if” takes the present; the past form belongs with “Would you mind if”.

fix.wrong: Would you mind waiting? — Yes, of course.
fix.right: Would you mind waiting? — No, not at all.
fix.why: “Mind” means object to, so agreement is expressed with a negative.

drill.name: Raise the register
drill.prompt: Make each request three times: direct, polite and very polite. Change the structure, not just the tone of voice.

dialogue.line: Would you mind giving me a hand with these boxes?
Not at all. Where are they going?
Upstairs. And could you possibly hold the door?
Sure. Do you mind if I take the lighter one?

grammar.sound: Requests rise at the end; the same words with a falling tone sound like an order. “Could you SEND it?” rising is a request, falling is an instruction.

grammar.name: Indirect requests and questions
grammar.short: Where is it? → Could you tell me where it is?
grammar.rule: An indirect question wraps the real question inside an introductory phrase. Inside the wrapper the clause returns to statement order: the subject comes before the verb, and the auxiliaries do, does and did disappear entirely.
form: Introducer + wh-word + subject + verb → Could you tell me where the station is?
With do/does: Where does she work? → Do you know where she works?
With past: Did he call? → I wonder whether he called.
Yes/no questions take if or whether: Is it open? → Do you know if it’s open?
Indirect requests: Could you ask him to call me? / I’d like to know when it closes.
notes: Never invert twice: “Do you know where is the station?” is the most common error at this level.
When do/does/did disappears, the tense and the third-person -s move onto the main verb: “where he lives”, “whether she called”.
If the whole sentence starts with a question it takes a question mark; if it starts with a statement (“I wonder…”) it takes a full stop.
Common introducers: Could you tell me…, Do you know…, I wonder…, I’d like to know…, Do you have any idea….
Indirect forms are the default with strangers, officials and customer service, and in written enquiries.
grammar.deep: Two grammars collide in these sentences and only one can win. A direct question uses inversion because inversion is English’s way of marking “this is a question”. In an indirect question the marking has already been done by the introducer, so the inner clause reverts to plain statement order. The clearest way to feel this is to notice that the inner clause is really the name of a piece of information: “where he lives” behaves like a noun, and you would never invert inside a noun phrase. The politeness effect follows from the same structure. By reporting your own curiosity instead of demanding an answer, you give the other person room to decline, and English speakers read that room as courtesy — which is why an indirect question is the safe choice whenever you do not know how your request will land.

chart.title: Direct to indirect
rows: Could you tell me where the exit is?
Do you know what time it opens?
I wonder if he called you.
Could you tell me if I can pay by card?
Do you have any idea who that is?
I’d like to know how much it is.

examples: Could you tell me where the meeting room is?
Do you know what time the last shuttle leaves?
I wonder whether she received my message.
I’d like to know how long the repair will take.
grammar.watch: After the introducer, write a statement: “…where the station is”, never “…where is the station”.
more: Could you tell me where the station is?
Do you know what time the office opens?
I wonder whether they received the invoice.
Would you mind telling me how much it costs?
Can you remember if she signed the form?
Do you have any idea why the flight was delayed?

fix.wrong: Could you tell me where is the station?
fix.right: Could you tell me where the station is?
fix.why: Inside an indirect question the clause takes statement order.

fix.wrong: Do you know what time does it open?
fix.right: Do you know what time it opens?
fix.why: The auxiliary “does” disappears and the verb takes the -s.

fix.wrong: I wonder that they received it.
fix.right: I wonder whether they received it.
fix.why: A yes/no question is wrapped with “if” or “whether”, not “that”.

drill.name: Wrap the question
drill.prompt: Turn each direct question into an indirect one, using a different introducer every time.
items: What time does the shop close?

dialogue.line: Excuse me, could you tell me where platform nine is?
Down the stairs and to the left.
Do you know if the train is running on time?
I’ve no idea, I’m afraid. Ask at the desk.

grammar.sound: The introducer carries the polite melody and the wrapped clause flattens out: “could you TELL me” rises, then “where the station is” stays level.

speaking.text: Each student asks the next for a favour, moving one step up the politeness scale each time. The last student must refuse politely with a reason.
One student staffs an information desk; the other needs six pieces of information. Every question must be indirect — a direct question loses a point.
Ask for three genuinely awkward favours (money, time off, a lift at midnight). Choose the politeness level deliberately and explain your choice.

tips: Match politeness to the size of the favour, not to your nerves.
After an introducer, the clause is a statement — delete do/does/did.
Always give a reason when you refuse.

quiz.q: Could you tell me when the next shuttle ___ ?
quiz.explain: Inside an indirect question the auxiliary disappears and the clause takes statement order: “when the next shuttle leaves”.

dynamics.name: Escalating favours
dynamics.how: Student A asks for progressively bigger favours; B must accept or refuse politely each time. When the favour becomes unreasonable, A must upgrade the structure to match.
dynamics.payoff: Register is chosen by the situation rather than by instruction.

dynamics.name: Information desk
dynamics.how: Half the class hold information cards (timetables, prices, opening hours); the other half must collect six answers using only indirect questions. Direct questions are refused.
dynamics.payoff: The refusal rule makes the structure necessary rather than decorative.

dynamics.name: Mind the answer
dynamics.how: Teacher asks “Would you mind…?” questions at speed; students must answer with a correct acceptance or refusal. Every “Yes, of course” meaning acceptance is corrected on the spot.
dynamics.payoff: Fixes the single most confusing answer pattern in the node.

dynamics.name: Awkward requests
dynamics.how: Groups draw a situation card (asking a neighbour, a boss, a stranger) and perform the same request three times for three listeners, then discuss which structures changed.
dynamics.payoff: Makes the politeness scale visible across one constant request.

writing.title: Four requests, four people
writing.brief: Write four short messages requesting the same thing from four different people: a close friend, a colleague, your manager and a stranger. Then write a formal enquiry containing three indirect questions.
criteria: Four different request structures, correctly graded by register.
Three indirect questions with statement word order.
At least one “Would you mind + -ing”.

homework.title: The politeness ladder
homework.task: Take five direct requests and rewrite each at three levels of politeness. Then convert eight direct questions into indirect ones, marking where you removed do, does or did.

test.q: Could you tell me when the next shuttle ___ ?
test.explain: Indirect questions take statement order with no auxiliary.

test.q: Would you mind ___ a few minutes?
test.explain: “Would you mind” takes a gerund.

test.q: Do you mind if I ___ the window?
test.explain: “Do you mind if” takes the present simple.

test.q: I wonder ___ they received the invoice.
test.explain: A yes/no question is wrapped with if or whether.

test.q: Would you mind moving your bag? — ___ .
test.explain: “Mind” means object, so a negative answer means agreement.

units.title: BLACK BOX
units.theme: Reconstructing a sequence of past events

overview.intro: Reading the flight recorder means putting events in order. The past continuous paints the background and gets interrupted by the simple past; the past perfect reaches back behind both to mark what had already happened. Together they let you narrate anything without a timeline on the wall.
goals: Contrast the past continuous and the simple past in narration.
Use the past perfect to mark the earlier of two past events.
Combine all three tenses in a single connected account.
overview.outcome: By the end you can narrate an incident in a full paragraph, with background, interruption and an earlier cause.

vocab.def: to stop someone or something in the middle of an action.
vocab.use: Transitive: “Sorry to interrupt you.” Noun: interruption. The past continuous is what gets interrupted.
examples: He interrupted me while I was speaking.
The alarm interrupted the meeting.
vocab.colloc: sorry to interrupt · constantly interrupt

vocab.def: to understand something suddenly and clearly.
vocab.use: Followed by a that-clause: “I realised that I had left it behind.” Often paired with the past perfect.
examples: I only realised the problem when it was too late.
She realised she had forgotten her keys.
vocab.colloc: suddenly realise · didn’t realise

vocab.def: before or at the moment that something else happened.
vocab.use: Almost always with the past perfect in the main clause: “By the time we arrived, it had finished.”
examples: By the time the ambulance came, he had recovered.
By the time I checked, the file had gone.
vocab.colloc: by the time we got there · by then

vocab.def: to stop working (a machine or vehicle).
vocab.use: Intransitive with no object: “The car broke down.” Different from “break up” (end a relationship).
examples: The engine broke down halfway.
Our system broke down twice last week.
vocab.colloc: break down on the road · a breakdown

vocab.def: in the end, after a long time or several problems.
vocab.use: A false friend for Spanish speakers: it does not mean “possibly”.
examples: Eventually they answered my email.
She eventually agreed to help.
vocab.colloc: eventually arrive · eventually gave up

vocab.def: at the same time, in another place.
vocab.use: An adverb, not a conjunction: it links sentences, not clauses. “Meanwhile, nobody had told the client.”
examples: Meanwhile, the passengers were still waiting.
I’ll call them; meanwhile, you check the log.
vocab.colloc: meanwhile · in the meantime

vocab.def: to investigate something.
vocab.use: Inseparable: “look into the problem”, “look into it”.
examples: They looked into the cause for weeks.
I’ll look into it this afternoon.
vocab.colloc: look into a matter · worth looking into

vocab.def: a person who saw an event; to see an event.
vocab.use: “A witness to the accident” with “to”. As a verb it takes a direct object: “She witnessed the crash.”
examples: Three witnesses had seen the same thing.
He witnessed the whole incident.
vocab.colloc: an eyewitness · a key witness

vocab.def: (of an alarm) to start ringing; (of a bomb) to explode.
vocab.use: Intransitive: “The alarm went off at three.” Also “go off” = food spoiling.
examples: The smoke alarm went off while I was cooking.
The fire alarm went off twice.
vocab.colloc: the alarm went off · go off suddenly

vocab.def: a period of waiting caused by a problem.
vocab.use: “A delay of two hours”, “without delay”. As a verb it takes -ing: “delayed leaving”.
examples: There had been a delay of two hours before we boarded.
The storm delayed all flights.
vocab.colloc: a slight delay · a long delay · without delay

vocab.def: during the period between two events.
vocab.use: Joins two past or future points and is useful in narration: “The engineer arrived at six. In the meantime, we had checked the logs.”
examples: The parts arrive on Friday. In the meantime, we’re using the spare.
She was delayed; in the meantime we started without her.
vocab.colloc: in the meantime · meanwhile · in the meantime, we…

grammar.name: Past continuous vs simple past
grammar.short: I was cooking when the alarm went off.
grammar.rule: The past continuous (was/were + -ing) describes an action in progress at a past moment — the background. The simple past describes a completed action — the event. In narration the simple past interrupts the past continuous.
form: Past continuous: was / were + -ing → At eight I was still working.
Interruption: past continuous + when + simple past → I was leaving when he called.
Parallel actions: While I was cooking, she was studying.
Negative / question: I wasn’t listening. / What were you doing at ten?
Scene setting with no interruption: It was raining and nobody was talking.
notes: “When” usually introduces the short completed action; “while” usually introduces the longer background one.
State verbs resist the continuous: know, believe, own, want, belong. Say “I knew”, not “I was knowing”.
Two past continuous clauses joined by “while” mean the actions overlapped completely.
The past continuous can express an interrupted plan: “I was going to call you, but I fell asleep.”
A story told entirely in the simple past has no background; one told entirely in the continuous has no events.
grammar.deep: Narration in English runs on two layers and the tenses keep them apart. The past continuous is the canvas — weather, moods, activities already under way — and the simple past is the paint, the events that move the story forward. If everything is in the simple past, nothing feels more important than anything else; if everything is in the continuous, nothing ever happens. There is also a subtlety in the interrupted use worth noticing: “I was walking to the station when I saw her” implies the walk was in progress and possibly not completed, while “I walked to the station and saw her” presents both actions as finished and sequential. Choosing the continuous is therefore a way of signalling incompleteness, and that small choice carries real narrative information.

rows: I was sleeping when the alarm rang.
While I was sleeping, the alarm rang.
She was cooking while I was working.
I woke up, showered and left.
It was raining and the streets were empty.
I was going to call, but I forgot.

examples: I was crossing the street when a car came round the corner.
While we were waiting for the shuttle, it started to rain.
What were you doing when the power went out?
She wasn’t paying attention, so she missed the announcement.
grammar.watch: Do not use the continuous with state verbs: “I was knowing him” must be “I knew him”.
more: I was crossing the street when a car came round the corner.
While we were waiting, it started to rain.
What were you doing when the power went out?
She wasn’t paying attention, so she missed the announcement.
They were arguing about the budget when the director walked in.
We were still testing at midnight.

fix.wrong: I was knowing him at that time.
fix.right: I knew him at that time.
fix.why: State verbs do not take the continuous.

fix.wrong: While I studied, the phone was ringing three times.
fix.right: While I was studying, the phone rang three times.
fix.why: The long background action is continuous; the short repeated event is simple.

fix.wrong: When I arrived, she cooked dinner.
fix.right: When I arrived, she was cooking dinner.
fix.why: The action already in progress at that moment must be continuous.

drill.name: Background and event
drill.prompt: Give each situation a continuous background and a simple-past interruption, then reverse the clause order and add the comma.

dialogue.line: What were you doing when the alarm went off?
I was running a diagnostic on bay two.
Did you see anyone?
No. While I was working, everyone else was in the briefing.

contrast.title: Three past tenses in a narrative
rows: While I was reading, she was cooking.
We used to meet on Fridays.

grammar.sound: “Was” and “were” reduce to /wəz/ and /wə/; the information sits in the -ing verb. “I was WORKing when it HAPPened.”

grammar.name: Past perfect
grammar.short: By the time we arrived, the ship had left.
grammar.rule: The past perfect (had + past participle) marks the earlier of two past events. It exists to establish order, which lets you narrate out of chronological sequence without confusing your listener.
form: Affirmative: had + past participle → The ship had already left.
Negative: hadn’t + participle → They hadn’t told anyone.
Question: Had you finished before she called?
With time markers: by the time, before, after, already, just, never, yet.
Reported speech: “I lost it.” → He said he had lost it.
notes: Use it only when the order matters or is not obvious. If “after” or “before” already shows the sequence, the simple past is enough: “After I sent it, she called.”
Adverb position: already, just and never go between “had” and the participle; yet goes at the end of a negative.
“By the time” almost always triggers the past perfect in the main clause: “By the time I checked, it had gone.”
It is also the tense of past causes and explanations: “I was exhausted because I hadn’t slept.”
In reported speech the past simple and present perfect both shift to the past perfect.
grammar.deep: Think of the past perfect as a step behind the story rather than as a tense of its own. Your narrative sits in the simple past, and whenever you need to reach back to something that happened before that point, the past perfect takes you there and then returns you. That is why it so often appears in a subordinate clause explaining why the main event happened: “She was furious because I had forgotten the meeting.” Because its only job is ordering, it becomes optional as soon as another word supplies the order, which is why over-using it makes prose feel heavy. The B1 skill is not producing the form — “had” plus a participle is mechanically simple — but knowing when the sequence genuinely needs marking, and recognising the reduced pronunciation (“I’d finished”) that makes it hard to hear in speech.

chart.title: Past perfect and its time markers
rows: She had just gone when I called.
I had never seen anything like it.
By the time we arrived, it had ended.
I was tired because I hadn’t slept.

examples: By the time the engineers arrived, the system had already restarted itself.
I couldn’t get in because I had left my card at home.
She had never flown before that day.
They hadn’t finished the checks yet when the storm hit.
grammar.watch: Use the past perfect only for the earlier event, and drop it when “before” or “after” already makes the order clear.
more: By the time we reached the gate, the shuttle had already left.
She told me she had never seen anything like it.
They hadn’t told anyone before the announcement.
I realised I had left my badge on the desk.
The room was empty; everyone had gone home.
Once we had checked the logs, the pattern was obvious.

fix.wrong: When I arrived, the train already left.
fix.right: When I arrived, the train had already left.
fix.why: The earlier of two past events takes the past perfect.

fix.wrong: I had gone to the shop and I had bought milk and I had come home.
fix.right: I went to the shop, bought milk and came home.
fix.why: A simple sequence in order needs no past perfect at all.

fix.wrong: After I had arrived, I had called her.
fix.right: After I had arrived, I called her.
fix.why: Only the earlier event takes the perfect; the later one is simple.

drill.name: Which came first
drill.prompt: Join each pair of events into one sentence, putting the earlier one in the past perfect and starting with the later one.
items: the meeting ended / we got there
he sent the file / I checked my inbox
the shop closed / we ran for it
they fixed it / the inspector came

dialogue.line: Why didn’t they wait?
By the time we arrived, they had already closed the doors.
Had nobody called them?
I’d sent a message, but it hadn’t gone through. In the meantime they’d given the seats away.

contrast.title: Past perfect or simple past
rows: an event told out of order
I left. I had woken up late.
She was tired; she hadn’t slept.
He said he had seen it.
After we had eaten, we left.

grammar.sound: “Had” contracts onto the subject — “I’d”, “she’d”, “they’d” — and disappears almost entirely. The tense is carried by the participle, so the participle must be clear.

speaking.text: Narrate a small accident or surprise. Set the scene in the past continuous, interrupt it twice with the simple past, and explain one cause with the past perfect.
Two students are witnesses to the same event and are questioned separately with “What were you doing at…?”. The class checks whether their accounts match.
Tell a story in six sentences that uses all three tenses at least twice each. Your partner flags any tense that does not earn its place.

tips: “When” takes the short event, “while” takes the long background.
Past perfect only for the earlier event — and only when the order matters.
State verbs never take a continuous form.

quiz.q: By the time we reached the gate, the shuttle ___ .
quiz.explain: The departure happened before the arrival, so the earlier event takes the past perfect.

dynamics.name: Alibi
dynamics.how: Two suspects agree on what they were doing between eight and ten, then are questioned separately. The class collects the answers and finds the contradiction.
dynamics.payoff: Produces a stream of past continuous questions with a genuine reason to listen.

dynamics.name: Flight recorder
dynamics.how: Groups receive six events on cards out of order and must narrate the incident in a fixed order, using the past perfect wherever an event is told out of sequence.
dynamics.payoff: The scrambled cards make the past perfect the only way to be clear.

dynamics.name: Freeze and interrupt
dynamics.how: A group mimes a scene and freezes; the class describes what everyone was doing. The teacher calls an interruption and the class narrates it in the simple past.
dynamics.payoff: Separates background from event physically before grammatically.

dynamics.name: By the time
dynamics.how: Each student completes ten “By the time I…” prompts about yesterday, then reads five to a partner who checks that both tenses are correct.
dynamics.payoff: The frame guarantees a two-event sentence every time.

writing.title: The incident report
writing.brief: Narrate something that went wrong. Set the scene in the past continuous, deliver the events in the simple past, and use the past perfect at least three times to explain what had already happened before it began.

Three past perfect verbs, at least one after “by the time”.
No past perfect in a straightforward chronological sequence.

homework.title: Order of events
homework.task: Write eight pairs of past events from your own week and join each pair into one sentence, putting the earlier event in the past perfect. Then write five sentences describing what you were doing at five specific times yesterday.

units.title: PROTOCOL

overview.intro: Every culture runs on rules nobody writes down. This sector gives you the grammar for describing them: noun phrases with relative clauses inside them, so you can name a complicated thing precisely, and the language of expectation — what is the custom, what you are supposed to do, what is acceptable.
goals: Build noun phrases that contain relative clauses.
Express customs and expectations with it’s the custom to, be supposed to, be expected to.
State what is and is not acceptable in a given situation.
overview.outcome: By the end you can brief a visitor on six unwritten rules of your country or workplace, each in a full, precise sentence.

vocab.def: a traditional way of behaving in a particular society.
vocab.use: Countable: “a local custom”. The phrase “it’s the custom to + verb” states a norm.
examples: It’s the custom to bring a small gift.
Local customs vary a lot between regions.
vocab.colloc: a local custom · an old custom · customs and traditions

vocab.def: expected to, according to a rule or an arrangement.
vocab.use: “You’re supposed to wear ID.” In the past it usually implies the rule was broken: “I was supposed to call her.”
examples: You’re supposed to check in online first.
We were supposed to start at nine.
vocab.colloc: supposed to be · not supposed to

vocab.def: good enough or allowed in a particular situation.
vocab.use: “It’s (not) acceptable to + verb”. More formal than “OK”, softer than “forbidden”.
examples: It’s not acceptable to arrive an hour late.
Is it acceptable to call after nine?
vocab.colloc: perfectly acceptable · socially acceptable

vocab.def: required by other people’s assumptions.
vocab.use: Passive with an infinitive: “Guests are expected to dress smartly.” Slightly more formal than “supposed to”.
examples: Employees are expected to attend the briefing.
You’re expected to tip in restaurants there.
vocab.colloc: widely expected to · expected to arrive

vocab.def: to upset someone by breaking a social rule.
vocab.use: Transitive: “It might offend your host.” Adjective: offensive. Noun: offence.
examples: Refusing food can offend some hosts.
I didn’t mean to offend anyone.
vocab.colloc: easily offended · cause offence

vocab.def: the standard or usual behaviour in a group.
vocab.use: Countable, often plural: “social norms”. “The norm” means the usual thing.
examples: Working from home is the norm now.
Every culture has its own norms.
vocab.colloc: social norms · the norm · break a norm

vocab.def: suitable for the situation.
vocab.use: “Appropriate for / to + noun”: “appropriate for a formal dinner”. Opposite: inappropriate.
examples: That’s not appropriate for a job interview.
Choose an appropriate greeting.
vocab.colloc: appropriate behaviour · perfectly appropriate

vocab.def: to disapprove of something mildly.
vocab.use: Usually passive: “Tipping is frowned on here.” Inseparable.
examples: Arriving early is frowned on in some cultures.
Loud phone calls are frowned on.
vocab.colloc: frowned on · frown upon

vocab.def: the rules of polite behaviour in a society or profession.
vocab.use: Uncountable: “business etiquette”, “the etiquette of gift-giving”.
examples: Email etiquette varies by company.
There’s a whole etiquette around greetings.
vocab.colloc: business etiquette · basic etiquette

vocab.def: to do something wrong without being punished.
vocab.use: Three parts, always with an object or -ing: “get away with arriving late”.
examples: You can get away with jeans on Fridays.
He got away with it because nobody checked.
vocab.colloc: get away with it · get away with murder

vocab.def: to disapprove of something without formally forbidding it.
vocab.use: Usually passive: “Arriving late is frowned upon here.” Ideal for describing unwritten rules.
examples: Eating at your desk is frowned upon in this office.
They frown upon casual dress at the head office.
vocab.colloc: frowned upon · generally frowned upon

vocab.def: a custom that everyone follows although nobody has stated it.
vocab.use: Takes a that-clause or a to-infinitive: “There’s an unwritten rule that you greet everyone.”
examples: There’s an unwritten rule about the last seat on the bus.
Most unwritten rules only become visible when you break one.
vocab.colloc: an unwritten rule · break an unwritten rule

grammar.name: Noun phrases containing relative clauses
grammar.short: the kind of behaviour that upsets people
grammar.rule: A noun phrase can carry a relative clause inside it, which lets you name something complicated in a single unit. The whole phrase then behaves as one noun and can be the subject or object of the sentence.
form: Head noun + relative clause: the sort of question that nobody wants to answer.
Common frames: the kind of…, the sort of…, the type of…, the one thing that…, anything that…, someone who….
Quantified heads: most people who live here · a lot of visitors who come in July.
As subject: The people who arrive first usually get the best seats.
As object: I avoid the kind of restaurant that has photos on the menu.
notes: The verb agrees with the head noun, not with the noun nearest to it: “The list of names that arrived is long.”
Keep the relative clause next to the noun it describes, or it will attach to the wrong one.
“The kind of / the sort of” takes a singular or plural noun according to what you mean: “the kind of person who…”, “the kinds of people who…”.
Indefinite heads — anything, something, someone, everyone — take “that” or nothing rather than “which”.
These phrases are how English builds precise definitions, so they dominate explanation and instruction.
grammar.deep: Once a relative clause can sit inside a noun phrase, you can name things you have no single word for, which is exactly what B1 conversation requires: “the sort of colleague who replies to emails at midnight”, “the kind of rule that nobody explains to you”. The engineering is simple — a head noun plus a clause that identifies it — but two things go wrong in practice. Agreement drifts, because a long phrase puts distance between the head noun and the verb, so learners write “the list of names are” when the subject is “the list”. And the clause detaches, ending up next to the wrong noun. A reliable check is to read the sentence with the whole noun phrase replaced by “it”: if the result still makes sense, the phrase is doing its job as a single unit.

chart.title: Building complex noun phrases
rows: whose desk is next to mine

examples: The kind of behaviour that annoys people most is interrupting.
Anything that isn’t written down is a custom you have to learn.
Most travellers who visit for the first time make the same mistake.
There’s one rule that nobody ever explains to newcomers.
grammar.watch: Make the verb agree with the head noun: “The list of rules that arrived is long”, not “are long”.
more: The kind of behaviour that annoys people most is interrupting.
Anything that isn’t written down is a custom you have to learn.
The one thing that visitors always get wrong is the greeting.
Most travellers who arrive for the first time make the same mistake.
The sort of question that nobody wants to answer is about money.
Somebody who has lived here for a year will still be surprised.

fix.wrong: The list of rules that arrived are long.
fix.right: The list of rules that arrived is long.
fix.why: The verb agrees with the head noun “list”, not with “rules”.

fix.wrong: The kind of person who they respect.
fix.right: The kind of person they respect.
fix.why: With an object clause you drop either the pronoun or the second subject, not neither.

fix.wrong: The thing what bothers me is the noise.
fix.right: The thing that bothers me is the noise.
fix.why: “What” cannot follow a noun; use “that”.

drill.name: Build the phrase
drill.prompt: Turn each idea into a long noun phrase with a relative clause inside it, then use it as the subject of a full sentence.

dialogue.line: What’s the thing that surprises people most here?
The kind of greeting you’re expected to give. Everyone, individually.
Even in an office?
Especially in an office. Anyone who skips it is remembered for it.

contrast.title: Frames that carry a relative clause
rows: the kind of book that sells

grammar.sound: The head noun takes the stress and the whole relative clause runs on unstressed behind it: “the KIND of behaviour that annoys people”.

grammar.name: Expectations: it’s the custom to, (not) supposed to, expected to, (not) acceptable to
grammar.short: You’re supposed to take your shoes off.
grammar.rule: These structures describe what people expect rather than what the law requires. “It’s the custom to” states a tradition, “be supposed to” and “be expected to” state an expectation attached to a person, and “it’s (not) acceptable to” judges whether a behaviour is allowed socially.
form: It’s the custom to + verb → It’s the custom to greet everyone individually.
subject + be supposed to + verb → You’re supposed to arrive ten minutes early.
subject + be expected to + verb → Guests are expected to bring something.
It’s (not) acceptable to + verb → It’s not acceptable to check your phone at dinner.
Negatives: You’re not supposed to smoke here. / It isn’t the custom to tip.
notes: “Be supposed to” in the past usually implies the expectation was not met: “I was supposed to call her yesterday.”
“Be expected to” is a passive, so it can name the expecting party with “by”: “Staff are expected by management to…”.
“It’s the custom to” describes a whole society; “be supposed to” describes an individual’s obligation.
These are softer than “must” and “have to”, which state rules rather than expectations — a useful distinction when advising visitors.
Add a hedge for accuracy: “generally”, “usually”, “in most places”. Cultural claims are safer when they are not absolute.
grammar.deep: Rules and expectations are different things, and B1 is where the distinction becomes expressible. “You must show your passport” is a regulation with a consequence; “you’re supposed to shake hands” is a social expectation whose only sanction is other people’s reaction. That is why these structures are the natural language of cultural briefing: they describe pressure without claiming legal force. Two of them deserve special attention. “Be supposed to” carries a strong implication of failure in the past — “I was supposed to send it” almost always means you did not — so use it carefully when reporting your own behaviour. And “it’s not acceptable to” is genuinely strong in English, close to a reprimand, so for milder disapproval reach for “it’s frowned on” or “people don’t usually”. Hedging is not weakness here; it is accuracy, because customs are rarely universal.

chart.title: Expressing expectations
rows: It’s the custom to bring flowers.
People usually arrive a bit late.
You’re supposed to book in advance.
Guests are expected to dress smartly.
It’s frowned on to leave early.
It’s not acceptable to shout at staff.

examples: In many offices you’re supposed to say good morning to everyone individually.
It’s the custom to take a small gift when you visit someone’s home.
Visitors are expected to remove their shoes at the door.
It’s generally not acceptable to arrive more than ten minutes late for dinner.
grammar.watch: “I was supposed to” usually means you did not do it. If you did, say “I had to”.
more: It’s the custom to bring something small when you’re invited.
You’re supposed to take your shoes off at the door.
Guests are expected to arrive a few minutes late, not early.
It isn’t acceptable to answer your phone during a meal.
We were supposed to submit the form last Friday.
It’s considered rude to ask what someone earns.

fix.wrong: You are supposed take your shoes off.
fix.right: You are supposed to take your shoes off.
fix.why: “Be supposed” always keeps the “to”.

fix.wrong: It’s the custom bringing a gift.
fix.right: It’s the custom to bring a gift.
fix.why: This frame takes an infinitive, not a gerund.

fix.wrong: You don’t suppose to smoke here.
fix.right: You’re not supposed to smoke here.
fix.why: The structure is passive: be + supposed to.

drill.name: Rules nobody wrote
drill.prompt: Describe each situation with three different expectation structures, one of them negative.

dialogue.line: Am I supposed to bring anything?
It’s the custom to bring something small — flowers, or a cake.
And what time?
Guests are expected to be ten minutes late. Arriving early isn’t really acceptable.

contrast.title: Expectation, not law
rows: It’s the custom to shake hands.
Staff are expected to wear badges.

grammar.sound: “Supposed to” is pronounced /səˈpəʊstə/ — the d disappears entirely and the two words fuse. Saying /səˈpəʊzd tuː/ marks the speaker as reading, not talking.

speaking.text: Brief a newcomer on six unwritten rules of your country or workplace, using a different expectation structure for each.
Describe five things you dislike using complex noun phrases only: “the kind of person who…”, “anything that…”.
Tell the group about a time you broke a social rule. Explain what you were supposed to do and what actually happened.

tips: Make the verb agree with the head noun, not the nearest noun.
“Supposed to” in the past implies you didn’t do it.
Hedge cultural claims — “usually”, “in most places” — they are rarely absolute.

quiz.q: We ___ to submit the form last Friday, but nobody told us.
quiz.explain: “Be supposed to” in the past expresses an expectation that was not met, so the past form “were supposed to” is correct.

dynamics.name: Culture briefing
dynamics.how: Each group prepares a two-minute briefing for a newcomer to their city, covering six expectations. Every point must use a different structure from the contrast table.
dynamics.payoff: The table becomes a production checklist, so the rarer frames appear.

dynamics.name: Rule or custom
dynamics.how: Teacher reads twenty statements; students sort them into RULE (must / have to) or CUSTOM (supposed to / the custom to) and justify any disagreement.
dynamics.payoff: Draws the line between law and expectation, which is the meaning of the node.

dynamics.name: The visitor’s mistake
dynamics.how: Each pair invents a visitor who breaks four unwritten rules in one day, then narrates the day and names each rule with a long noun phrase.
dynamics.payoff: Combines both grammar points inside one story.

dynamics.name: Definition chain
dynamics.how: Groups define five abstract nouns (politeness, punctuality, hospitality) using “the kind of … that …” frames, then compare definitions with another group.
dynamics.payoff: Long noun phrases become necessary rather than optional.

writing.title: What nobody tells you
writing.brief: Write a short guide to the unwritten rules of a place you know well. Name each rule with a noun phrase containing a relative clause, then state the expectation with a different structure each time.
criteria: Four noun phrases with relative clauses inside them, correctly agreeing.
Five expectation structures, at least three different ones.
One past expectation with “was/were supposed to”.

homework.title: Six rules, six frames
homework.task: List six unwritten rules from your workplace, school or family. Express each one twice: once with a long noun phrase and once with an expectation structure. Mark any that would actually be a “have to”.

test.explain: A past expectation that was not met takes “were supposed to”.

test.explain: The verb agrees with the head noun “list”.
