units.title: MALFUNCTION
units.theme: Describing what is broken and what it needs

overview.intro: Something is always broken on a working ship. This sector gives you the two halves of a repair report: describing the fault, using past participles as adjectives and the right nouns, and stating the remedy with need + gerund, need + passive infinitive, and keep + gerund for problems that will not go away.
goals: Describe faults with past participles as adjectives and with problem nouns.
State what is required with need + gerund and need + passive infinitive.
Describe recurring faults with keep + gerund.
overview.outcome: By the end you can report five faults precisely and say what each one needs, in the register a technician would accept.

vocab.def: with a line of damage but not in pieces.
vocab.use: Before a noun (“a cracked screen”) or after “be” (“the screen is cracked”).
examples: The screen is cracked in the corner.
There’s a cracked tile in the bathroom.
vocab.colloc: a cracked screen · badly cracked

vocab.def: with surface marks / with a hollow from an impact.
vocab.use: Both work as adjectives: “a scratched lens”, “a dented door”.
examples: The lens arrived scratched.
The panel is slightly dented.
vocab.colloc: badly scratched · a dented bumper

vocab.def: an escape of liquid or gas through a hole.
vocab.use: Noun: “a leak in the pipe”. Verb: “the pipe is leaking”.
examples: There’s a leak under the sink.
The coolant tank has been leaking for days.
vocab.colloc: a slow leak · fix a leak · leaking pipe

vocab.def: a mark that is difficult to remove.
vocab.use: Noun: “a coffee stain”. Adjective form: stained. Verb: “it stained the carpet”.
examples: There’s a stain on the seat cover.
The upholstery is badly stained.
vocab.colloc: a stubborn stain · remove a stain

vocab.def: not firmly fixed in place.
vocab.use: Careful with pronunciation and spelling: “loose” (adjective) versus “lose” (verb).
examples: One of the handles is loose.
There’s a loose wire behind the panel.
vocab.colloc: a loose screw · come loose

vocab.def: not working correctly because of a defect.
vocab.use: Before a noun: “a faulty sensor”. The noun is “fault” or “defect”.
examples: We received a faulty unit.
The fault is in the wiring, not the software.
vocab.colloc: a faulty component · a manufacturing fault

vocab.def: to make something work again.
vocab.use: “Fix” is everyday, “repair” is slightly more formal and used for larger jobs.
examples: It needs fixing before Monday.
The panel has to be repaired, not replaced.
vocab.colloc: fix a problem · repair the damage

vocab.def: to put a new thing in place of an old one.
vocab.use: “Replace X with Y”: “replace the battery with a new one”. Noun: replacement.
examples: The filter needs to be replaced every month.
We replaced the whole unit.
vocab.colloc: replace a part · a replacement unit

vocab.def: to do something repeatedly or continuously.
vocab.use: Followed only by -ing: “it keeps crashing”. “Keep on + -ing” adds insistence.
examples: The engine keeps cutting out.
It keeps making a strange noise.
vocab.colloc: keeps happening · keep on trying

vocab.def: a written promise to repair or replace a product.
vocab.use: Countable: “under warranty”, “a two-year warranty”.
examples: It’s still under warranty.
The warranty doesn’t cover accidental damage.
vocab.colloc: under warranty · a limited warranty

vocab.def: to become unusable through long use.
vocab.use: Separable, and the participle “worn out” works as an adjective: “worn-out tyres”.
examples: The seals wear out after about two years.
These brushes are completely worn out.
vocab.colloc: wear out · worn out · wear it out

grammar.name: Describing problems with past participles as adjectives and with nouns
grammar.short: The screen is cracked. There’s a crack in the screen.
grammar.rule: English describes a fault in two parallel ways: with a past participle used as an adjective, which focuses on the state of the object, and with a problem noun, which names the fault itself. Both are correct and they are often interchangeable.
form: Participle after be: The screen is cracked. / The seat is stained.
Participle before a noun: a cracked screen · a stained seat · a dented panel.
Problem noun with there is/are: There’s a crack in the screen. / There are two dents.
Problem noun with have: The screen has a crack in it.
Negative state: It isn’t working. / It doesn’t work.
notes: Participles keep their irregular forms: broken, torn, worn, bent, burnt, frozen.
Some faults exist only as nouns (a leak, a scratch, a hole, a stain, a dent) and some only as participles (jammed, blocked).
With “there is / there are”, the number agrees with the noun: “There’s a dent”, “There are three dents”.
Add a location and a degree for a useful report: “badly cracked in the top corner”.
“Broken” covers both “in pieces” and “not working”, so add detail when the difference matters.
grammar.deep: A repair report is judged on precision, and English gives you two grammatical routes to it. The participle route puts the object first and its state second — “the panel is dented” — which suits a checklist of components. The noun route names the defect and locates it — “there’s a dent in the panel” — which suits a description of damage where the number and position matter. Learning both means you can vary a list of faults instead of repeating one pattern six times. Two practical notes: not every fault has both forms, so “a leak” has no participle equivalent and “jammed” has no common noun, and the participles are irregular often enough that they need memorising alongside their verbs. Finally, a good report always adds degree and location, because “cracked” and “badly cracked along the bottom edge” lead to very different responses.

chart.title: Two ways of describing the same fault
rows: There’s a crack in the screen.
There’s a dent in the door.
There are scratches on the lens.
There’s a stain on the seat.
There’s a tear in the cover.
There’s a leak in the pipe.
There’s a blockage in the drain.

examples: The rear panel is badly dented and one of the clips is broken.
There’s a small crack in the housing and a leak underneath.
Two of the seats are stained and the armrest is loose.
The connector isn’t damaged, but the cable is worn where it bends.
grammar.watch: Use the correct irregular participle: torn, worn, broken, bent — not “teared” or “breaked”.
more: The rear panel is badly dented and one of the clips is broken.
There’s a small crack in the housing and a leak underneath.
Two of the seats are stained and the armrest is loose.
The cable looks worn and the connector is bent.
We found a scratch on the lens and a chip in the frame.
The display is faulty, and there’s a rattle when it moves.

fix.wrong: The screen is cracking.
fix.right: The screen is cracked.
fix.why: A state of damage takes the past participle; the -ing form describes an action happening now.

fix.wrong: There is a broken in the handle.
fix.right: The handle is broken. / There’s a break in the handle.
fix.why: “Broken” is the adjective; the noun is “break”.

fix.wrong: The sleeve is teared.
fix.right: The sleeve is torn.
fix.why: Irregular participle: tear → torn.

drill.name: Two ways to report it
drill.prompt: Describe each fault twice: once with a past participle adjective and once with a problem noun.

dialogue.line: What’s wrong with it?
The casing is cracked and there’s a scratch on the lens.
Anything else?
The button is loose. There’s also a rattle inside, which worries me more.

grammar.sound: Two-syllable participle adjectives keep the /ɪd/: “dented”, “stained” is one syllable, “scratched” is one. Adding a syllable to “scratched” marks it as a learner error immediately.

grammar.name: Need + gerund, need + passive infinitive, and keep + gerund
grammar.short: It needs fixing. / It needs to be fixed. / It keeps crashing.
grammar.rule: When a thing requires an action, English offers two equivalent structures: “need + gerund” and “need + passive infinitive”. Both mean the same thing and the object is the subject. “Keep + gerund” describes a fault that happens repeatedly.
form: need + gerund: The filter needs replacing.
need + passive infinitive: The filter needs to be replaced.
With a person as subject: I need to replace the filter. (active, ordinary need)
keep + gerund: The engine keeps stalling.
keep on + gerund for insistence: It keeps on doing it.
notes: “Needs replacing” and “needs to be replaced” are interchangeable; the gerund version is more spoken, the passive infinitive slightly more formal.
Do not mix them: “needs to replacing” and “needs be replaced” are both wrong.
When a person is the subject, “need” takes an ordinary active infinitive: “I need to check the wiring.”
“Keep” is always followed by -ing, never an infinitive: “it keeps crashing”, not “it keeps to crash”.
“Want” can replace “need” in the gerund pattern in informal British English: “that door wants painting”.
grammar.deep: These two structures solve a small puzzle: how to say that something requires an action without naming who will do it. “The filter needs replacing” and “the filter needs to be replaced” both leave the technician out of the sentence, which is exactly right in a fault report where the agent is irrelevant. The trap is hybrid forms — “needs to replacing”, “needs be replaced” — which come from starting one pattern and finishing the other, so practise them as two separate whole units rather than as variations. “Keep + gerund” adds the dimension that matters most in diagnostics: recurrence. A fault that happens once and a fault that keeps happening call for different responses, and English marks the difference with this single verb. Note that “keep” also means “continue”, so context decides between “it keeps crashing” (repeatedly) and “keep pressing” (continuously).

chart.title: Need and keep patterns
rows: The brakes need to be adjusted.
I need to adjust the brakes.
needs to replacing ✘ / keeps to crash ✘

examples: The coolant tank needs draining before the next flight.
Two of the seals need to be replaced, and the third needs cleaning.
The display keeps freezing whenever we restart the system.
I need to run the diagnostics again, because it keeps failing the same test.
grammar.watch: “Needs fixing” or “needs to be fixed” — never “needs to fixing”. And “keep” always takes -ing.
more: The filter needs replacing before the next inspection.
The report needs to be signed by two people.
It keeps crashing whenever I open a second window.
These boots need cleaning; they don’t need replacing yet.
The door keeps sticking in wet weather.
This section needs to be rewritten, not just corrected.

fix.wrong: The filter needs to replace.
fix.right: The filter needs replacing. / The filter needs to be replaced.
fix.why: With a thing as subject, use a gerund or a passive infinitive.

fix.wrong: It keeps to crash.
fix.right: It keeps crashing.
fix.why: “Keep” is always followed by a gerund.

fix.wrong: I need replacing the filter.
fix.right: I need to replace the filter.
fix.why: With a person as subject the ordinary active infinitive is correct.

drill.name: Needs doing
drill.prompt: State what each object requires, twice — with a gerund and with a passive infinitive — then add a “keeps + -ing” complaint about it.

dialogue.line: Is it worth repairing?
The belt needs replacing, and the motor needs to be checked.
And the noise?
It keeps overheating. That’s what causes it.

grammar.sound: “Needs replacing” links into /niːdzrɪˈpleɪsɪŋ/ with no pause, and the stress falls on the gerund, which is the new information.

speaking.text: Report five faults in a room, a vehicle or a device. Describe each one twice — once with a participle, once with a noun — then say what it needs.
One student is a customer with three problems, the other is support. The customer must use “need + gerund” and “keep + gerund” at least twice each.
Describe a recurring problem in your daily life without naming the cause. The group asks questions and proposes what needs to be done.

tips: Two routes to the same report: “is cracked” or “there’s a crack in”.

units.title: IMPACT
units.theme: What is being done, what caused it, and why

overview.intro: When the action matters more than the actor, the passive takes over. This sector covers the passive in the present continuous and present perfect — the tenses of work in progress and results so far — together with the prepositions that assign cause, and the infinitive clauses that express purpose.
goals: Form the passive in the present continuous and present perfect.
Use prepositions of cause: because of, due to, as a result of, thanks to.
Express purpose and result with infinitive clauses and phrases.
overview.outcome: By the end you can describe an ongoing situation, name its causes and state what is being done about it, in the register of a report.

vocab.def: already happening, in progress.
vocab.use: With “be”: “Repairs are under way.” Two words in British English.
examples: An investigation is already under way.
Construction has been under way since March.
vocab.colloc: already under way · get under way

vocab.def: to perform or complete a task or study.
vocab.use: Separable: “carry out a survey”, “carry it out”. Very common in the passive.
examples: Tests are being carried out this week.
The repairs were carried out overnight.
vocab.colloc: carry out research · carry out an inspection

vocab.def: because of.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or -ing, never a clause: “due to heavy rain”, not “due to it rained”.
examples: The delay was due to a technical fault.
Due to demand, we’ve added a second session.
vocab.colloc: due to bad weather · largely due to

vocab.def: caused by.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun: “as a result of the storm”. The adverb version is “as a result”.
examples: Two flights were cancelled as a result of the storm.
As a result, we lost a whole day.
vocab.colloc: as a result of · as a direct result of

vocab.def: because of — usually with a positive result.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun: “thanks to the crew”. Can be ironic: “thanks to the delay, we missed it”.
examples: Thanks to the new system, waiting times have halved.
We finished early thanks to Ana.
vocab.colloc: thanks to your help · largely thanks to

vocab.def: a result, usually a serious one.
vocab.use: “The consequences of + noun”, “as a consequence”. More formal than “result”.
examples: The consequences of the fault are still being assessed.
As a consequence, the launch was postponed.
vocab.colloc: serious consequences · face the consequences

vocab.def: to influence something / the result of an influence.
vocab.use: “Affect” is the verb, “effect” the noun: “The delay affected everyone”, “the effect was serious”.
examples: The storm affected all departures.
The new rule has had a big effect.
vocab.colloc: seriously affect · have an effect on

vocab.def: to be examined and judged.
vocab.use: Common in reports: “The damage is being assessed.” Noun: assessment.
examples: The damage is still being assessed.
Applications have been assessed by two reviewers.
vocab.colloc: be assessed by · a full assessment

vocab.def: still happening.
vocab.use: Before a noun: “an ongoing investigation”. Do not use after “be” in careful writing.
examples: It’s an ongoing problem.
The ongoing repairs will finish on Friday.
vocab.colloc: an ongoing investigation · ongoing support

vocab.def: a more formal way of saying “to” when giving a reason.
vocab.use: “In order to + verb”, and the negative “in order not to + verb”.
examples: We closed the deck in order to carry out repairs.
She whispered in order not to wake him.
vocab.colloc: in order to · in order not to · so as to

grammar.name: Passive in the present continuous and present perfect; prepositions of cause
grammar.short: The hull is being repaired. Three panels have been replaced.
grammar.rule: The passive is formed with “be” plus a past participle, and the tense lives entirely in “be”. The present continuous passive describes work in progress; the present perfect passive describes what has been completed so far. Prepositions of cause then attach the reason.
form: Present continuous passive: is / are being + participle → The system is being upgraded.
Present perfect passive: has / have been + participle → Three faults have been fixed.
Negative / question: It isn’t being repaired. / Has it been tested?
With by + agent, only when the agent matters: The report has been signed by the director.
Cause: because of / due to / as a result of / thanks to / owing to + noun.
notes: The tense sits in “be”, so the second word is always a participle: “is being repaired”, “has been repaired”.
Drop “by + agent” when the agent is unknown, obvious or irrelevant — which is most of the time in reports.
“Because” takes a clause, while “because of”, “due to”, “as a result of” and “thanks to” take a noun or gerund.
Only transitive verbs have a passive: happen, arrive and occur cannot be passivised.
“Being” appears only in the continuous passive; “has being repaired” is always wrong.
grammar.deep: The passive is a spotlight rather than a politeness device. Every sentence has a topic, and English puts the topic in the subject position; when the interesting thing is the object of the action, the passive keeps it at the front and preserves the flow of a paragraph. That is why status reports live in these two tenses: the present continuous passive tells your reader what is happening right now (“the pipes are being replaced”), and the present perfect passive tells them the score so far (“two sections have been completed”). The prepositions of cause complete the picture, and the only real difficulty is grammatical category: “because” introduces a clause, everything else introduces a noun. Getting that wrong produces “due to it was raining”, which is the commonest cause error at this level. If you can see a subject and a verb, you need “because”.

chart.title: Passive forms and cause expressions
rows: We stopped because the pump failed.
We stopped due to a pump failure.
Delays occurred as a result of the storm.
Thanks to the crew, nobody was hurt.
due to it failed ✘ / has being cleaned ✘

examples: The navigation module is being replaced because of a software fault.
Three of the six sensors have already been recalibrated.
Due to the delay, the inspection has been postponed until Monday.
Thanks to the maintenance team, the system has been running without errors for a week.
grammar.watch: “Because” + clause, “because of / due to” + noun. And the participle after “be”: “has been repaired”, never “has being repaired”.
more: The navigation module is being replaced because of a software fault.
Three of the six sensors have already been recalibrated.
Due to the delay, the inspection has been postponed.
The hull is being inspected while we speak.
Nothing has been decided yet, as far as I know.
Two reports have been filed and a third is being written.

fix.wrong: The system has being upgraded.
fix.right: The system has been upgraded.
fix.why: The present perfect passive is has/have been + participle.

fix.wrong: The bay is repairing at the moment.
fix.right: The bay is being repaired at the moment.
fix.why: Work in progress on the subject requires the continuous passive.

fix.wrong: It was cancelled because of the weather was bad.
fix.right: It was cancelled because the weather was bad.
fix.why: “Because of” takes a noun; a clause needs plain “because”.

drill.name: Progress report
drill.prompt: Report the state of each job twice: what is being done now, and what has already been done.

dialogue.line: Where are we with bay two?
The panel is being replaced now. Two of the sensors have already been recalibrated.
Why the delay?
Due to a faulty relay. The whole line had to be shut down.

grammar.sound: “Been” is unstressed and reduced to /bɪn/, while “being” keeps two clear syllables. That difference is the only audible signal between the two tenses.

grammar.name: Infinitive clauses and phrases
grammar.short: We closed the bay to carry out repairs.
grammar.rule: An infinitive clause expresses purpose, intention or a further comment. Most often it answers “why?”: “to + verb”, or the more formal “in order to / so as to”. It can also follow adjectives and nouns to complete their meaning.
form: Purpose: I called to confirm the time. / in order to confirm / so as to confirm.
Negative purpose: in order not to / so as not to → I left early so as not to miss it.
With a different subject: for + object + infinitive → We closed the bay for the engineers to work safely.
After adjectives: difficult to explain · ready to launch · the first to arrive.
After nouns: the decision to postpone · a chance to speak · nothing to do.
notes: “For + verb” is impossible: never “for to open”. Purpose is “to open”; function is “for opening”.
The negative purpose form is “in order not to”, not “to not”: “in order not to lose data”.
When the two clauses have different subjects, English uses “for + object + infinitive”: “There’s too much noise for me to concentrate.”
Some nouns and adjectives take a fixed infinitive: “the ability to”, “a decision to”, “likely to”, “willing to”.
A bare “to + verb” is the default; “in order to” and “so as to” raise the register.
grammar.deep: Infinitives look forward, which is why they carry purpose so naturally: “to + verb” always names something not yet achieved. That single idea explains most of the pattern’s uses — reasons (“I came to help”), plans (“a decision to wait”), potential (“ready to launch”) and evaluations (“hard to explain”). Two structures raise your precision. The negative purpose form must be “in order not to” or “so as not to”, because a bare “to not” is not accepted in careful English, and this is the error examiners notice. And “for + object + infinitive” solves the problem of two different subjects, letting you say who the purpose is for: “We rescheduled the briefing for the new crew to attend.” Once you control that pattern, you can express purpose in sentences where the person acting is not the person planning.

chart.title: Infinitive clause uses
rows: We left early in order not to be late.
It’s too dark for us to work.
The system is ready to launch.
There was no time to check.

examples: The bay has been sealed in order to carry out pressure tests.
There isn’t enough time for the team to run a full diagnostic.
She was the first to notice that the readings had changed.
We postponed the launch so as not to risk a second failure.
grammar.watch: Never write “for + infinitive” for purpose, and use “in order not to”, not “to not”.
more: We closed the bay to carry out repairs.
I called in order to confirm the booking.
She left early so as not to miss the last train.
The form is designed to be filled in online.
They printed a second copy for the auditors to take away.
There’s nothing left to decide.

fix.wrong: I called for confirm the time.
fix.right: I called to confirm the time.
fix.why: Purpose takes an infinitive, never “for + verb”.

fix.wrong: We left early for not miss the train.
fix.right: We left early so as not to miss the train.
fix.why: The negative purpose forms are “in order not to” and “so as not to”.

fix.wrong: This tool is for cut metal.
fix.right: This tool is for cutting metal.
fix.why: Function takes “for + -ing”; purpose takes “to + verb”.

drill.name: Why did you do it
drill.prompt: Answer each question three ways: with “to”, with “in order to”, and with a negative purpose.
items: why did you save two copies
why did you call the supplier
why did you take the earlier train
why did you check it twice

dialogue.line: Why did you shut the whole line down?
To isolate the fault. It was faster than testing each unit.
And the second copy?
That’s for the auditors to take away, so as not to lose the original.

contrast.title: Purpose, function, reason
rows: in order to / so as to
in order not to / so as not to
so as not to wake him

grammar.sound: The “to” of purpose reduces to /tə/ and attaches to the verb: “to confirm” is /təkənˈfɜːm/. Full “to” /tuː/ sounds like a list, not a purpose.

speaking.text: Report on a project in six sentences: three in the present continuous passive, three in the present perfect passive. Add a cause to each.
Give six statements of cause, alternating between “because” and a preposition of cause. Your partner corrects any mismatch.
Explain five decisions using infinitive clauses of purpose, including one negative purpose and one with “for + object”.

tips: The tense lives in “be”; the second word is always a participle.
“Because” + clause, “due to” + noun.
Negative purpose is “in order not to”, never “to not”.

quiz.q: The engine ___ at the moment, ___ a faulty sensor.
quiz.explain: Work in progress takes the present continuous passive, and “due to” is followed by a noun phrase.

dynamics.name: Status board
dynamics.how: Each group runs an imaginary project and produces a status board with six lines: three in the continuous passive, three in the perfect passive. Other groups ask two questions each.
dynamics.payoff: The two tenses sit side by side, which is where the confusion lives.

dynamics.payoff: Guessing generates purpose clauses in quantity.

dynamics.how: Teacher reads a cause as either a clause or a noun; students respond with the correctly matched connector and the full sentence.
dynamics.payoff: Removes the most persistent error in this node.

dynamics.how: Pairs write eight signs for a workplace using passives and purpose clauses (“This door is kept locked to prevent…”), then post and read them.
dynamics.payoff: Puts both structures in the genre that actually uses them.

writing.brief: Write a progress update on a project. Report what is being done now and what has already been completed, in the passive, and explain the purpose of at least three decisions with infinitive clauses.

Three purpose clauses, one of them negative.
Correct choice between because and because of throughout.

test.q: The engine ___ at the moment, ___ a faulty sensor.
test.explain: Work in progress takes the continuous passive, and a noun takes “due to”.

test.q: Three faults ___ since Monday.
test.explain: The present perfect passive is have been + participle.

Under it, two rows: IS BEING + participle (now) and HAS BEEN + participle (result), with a clock drawn beside the first and a tick beside the second.

units.title: COURSE CHANGE
units.theme: Stating a preference, and explaining the method

overview.intro: Two practical structures. “Would rather” and “would prefer” let you state a preference precisely, including preferences about what other people do. “By + gerund” explains the method — how a result is achieved — which is the backbone of every instruction and every explanation of process.
goals: State preferences with would rather and would prefer, in the affirmative, negative and interrogative.
Express preferences about other people’s actions with would rather + past.
Explain method and means with by + gerund and with + noun.
overview.outcome: By the end you can negotiate a plan by stating preferences precisely, and explain how any result was achieved in three steps.

vocab.def: to prefer to do something.
vocab.use: Always “would rather + base verb”: “I’d rather stay.” Negative: “I’d rather not”.
examples: I’d rather walk than wait for the bus.
I’d rather not talk about it.
vocab.colloc: I’d rather not · would you rather

vocab.def: to prefer — followed by an infinitive or a noun.
vocab.use: “I’d prefer to walk”, “I’d prefer coffee”. With a comparison: “I’d prefer tea to coffee”.
examples: I’d prefer to meet in the morning.
She’d prefer the earlier flight.
vocab.colloc: I’d prefer to · I’d prefer not to

vocab.def: to be enthusiastic about something.
vocab.use: “Keen on + noun / -ing”: “keen on cycling”. Often negative: “I’m not keen on it”.
examples: I’m not keen on flying at night.
She’s very keen on the idea.
vocab.colloc: not too keen on · keen on the idea

vocab.def: a way of doing something.
vocab.use: Countable: “a reliable method”. “The method of + -ing” or “a method for + -ing”.
examples: There’s a faster method of doing this.
We changed our method halfway through.
vocab.colloc: a reliable method · a new method

vocab.def: the way or the tools by which something is achieved.
vocab.use: Same form in singular and plural: “a means of transport”, “by means of”. Never “a mean”.
examples: Email is the quickest means of reaching them.
We got in by means of a side door.
vocab.colloc: a means of transport · by means of

vocab.def: to calculate or find a solution; to end well.
vocab.use: Separable: “work out the cost”, “work it out”. Also intransitive: “it worked out fine”.
examples: We worked out the cost by adding the fees.
It all worked out in the end.
vocab.colloc: work out a solution · work it out

vocab.def: to reduce the amount of something.
vocab.use: Three parts, followed by a noun or -ing: “cut down on sugar”, “cut down on spending”.
examples: We cut costs by cutting down on travel.
She’s cutting down on coffee.
vocab.colloc: cut down on spending · cut down on waste

vocab.def: slowly, over a period of time.
vocab.use: Usually before the verb: “Things gradually improved.” Useful in method descriptions.
examples: You can improve gradually by practising daily.
The noise gradually stopped.
vocab.colloc: gradually increase · gradually improve

vocab.def: in place of.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or -ing, never an infinitive: “instead of waiting”.
examples: We saved time by taking the tunnel instead of the bridge.
Instead of complaining, do something.
vocab.colloc: instead of that · rather than

vocab.def: good enough to justify the effort.
vocab.use: “Worth + -ing”: “worth trying”. Never “worth to try”.
examples: It’s worth checking the manual first.
That approach isn’t worth trying again.
vocab.colloc: well worth doing · not worth it

vocab.def: to justify the cost, time or trouble involved.
vocab.use: Followed by a gerund when the activity is named: “It’s worth checking twice.”
examples: The extra hour was worth it.
It’s worth asking before you buy.
vocab.colloc: well worth it · not worth it · worth doing

grammar.name: Would rather and would prefer
grammar.short: I’d rather walk. / I’d prefer to walk. / I’d rather you didn’t.
grammar.rule: Both express preference. “Would rather” is followed by a base verb; “would prefer” by an infinitive or a noun. For a preference about someone else’s behaviour, “would rather” takes a clause with a past form.
form: I’d rather + base verb → I’d rather stay here.
I’d rather + base verb + than + base verb → I’d rather walk than drive.
I’d prefer + to + verb → I’d prefer to stay here.
I’d prefer + noun (+ to + noun) → I’d prefer tea to coffee.
About someone else: I’d rather you didn’t smoke here. (past form, present meaning)
notes: “Would rather” takes no “to”: “I’d rather go”, never “I’d rather to go”.
The comparison word differs: “rather … than”, but “prefer … to”. Mixing them produces “prefer than”, which is wrong.
Negatives attach to “rather” and “prefer”, not to the verb: “I’d rather not go”, “I’d prefer not to go”.
“I’d rather you + past form” is the polite way to ask someone to change their behaviour — the past form signals unreality, not past time.
Questions: “Would you rather stay or go?” and “Which would you prefer?”
grammar.deep: These two structures do the same job with different grammar, and the errors come from crossing them. “Rather” is an adverb attached directly to a bare verb, so nothing comes between them; “prefer” is a full verb, so it needs “to” before another verb. Their comparison words are equally fixed: “rather … than” and “prefer … to”. Once those are automatic, the interesting form is “I’d rather you didn’t”, which uses a past tense with present meaning — the same unreality marker you meet in second conditionals and after “wish”. It is one of the most useful polite structures in English, because it expresses a request as your own preference rather than as an instruction: “I’d rather you called before coming” is a great deal gentler than “don’t come without calling”, and native speakers use it constantly to manage other people’s behaviour without confrontation.

chart.title: Would rather / would prefer
rows: I’d prefer it if you didn’t stay.

examples: I’d rather take the night shuttle than wait until morning.
She’d prefer to review the figures before the meeting.
I’d rather not comment until the report is finished.
I’d rather you told me now than in a week’s time.
grammar.watch: “Rather” takes a bare verb and “than”; “prefer” takes “to + verb” and “to”. Never “prefer than”.
more: I’d rather take the night shuttle than wait until morning.
She’d prefer to review the figures before the meeting.
I’d rather not comment until the report is finished.
I’d rather you didn’t mention it to the client.
Would you rather meet on Thursday or Friday?
He’d prefer a written summary to a long call.

fix.wrong: I’d rather to stay here.
fix.right: I’d rather stay here.
fix.why: “Would rather” takes a bare infinitive.

fix.wrong: I’d prefer than walk.
fix.right: I’d prefer to walk.
fix.why: “Prefer” takes “to + verb”, never “than”.

fix.wrong: I’d rather you don’t say anything.
fix.right: I’d rather you didn’t say anything.
fix.why: A preference about someone else’s behaviour takes the past form.

drill.name: Two options, one preference
drill.prompt: State a preference between each pair twice: once with “would rather … than” and once with “would prefer … to”.

dialogue.line: Shall we do the review by video?
I’d rather meet in person than talk over a bad line.
Thursday, then?
I’d prefer Friday, if that works. And I’d rather you didn’t invite the whole team.

grammar.sound: “I’d rather” collapses to /aɪdˈrɑːðə/, and “rather” carries the stress. Without the contracted “d”, the sentence sounds like a statement of fact rather than a preference.

grammar.name: By + gerund to describe how to do things
grammar.short: You can save fuel by flying lower.
grammar.rule: “By + gerund” names the method: the action through which a result is achieved. It answers the question “how?”. The related structure “with + noun” names the instrument rather than the action.
form: Result + by + gerund → We reduced costs by cutting travel.
By + gerund first, with a comma → By checking twice, we avoided the error.
Negative method: by not + gerund → You save time by not repeating the test.
Instrument: with + noun → Open it with a screwdriver.
Without a method: without + gerund → We finished without asking for help.
notes: “By” is a preposition, so the verb after it always takes -ing: “by adding”, never “by add” or “by to add”.
“By” names an action; “with” names a tool or a material: “by cutting the cable” versus “with a knife”.
The negative goes before the gerund: “by not sending it twice”.
“Through” can replace “by” with abstract nouns: “through careful planning”.
Do not confuse this “by” with the passive agent “by”, which is followed by a noun: “written by an engineer”.
grammar.deep: “By + gerund” is the grammar of method, and it is what turns a list of actions into an explanation. Compare “we cut costs — we reduced travel” with “we cut costs by reducing travel”: the second states the causal link explicitly, and that link is exactly what a reader or examiner is looking for in an explanation. Because “by” is a preposition, the gerund is obligatory, which makes this one of the safest structures in English once you have internalised it. Two refinements are worth having. The contrast with “with” is real: “with” introduces the instrument (“with a spanner”) while “by” introduces the action (“by tightening the bolts”), and using the wrong one is immediately noticeable. And the negative form, “by not + gerund”, lets you explain a method that consists of avoidance, which is often the most useful advice you can give.

chart.title: Method, instrument and absence
rows: We saved time by automating it.
You avoid errors by not rushing.
It was designed by our team.

examples: We cut the maintenance time in half by pre-loading the diagnostics.
By checking the log first, you avoid repeating the whole test.
You can improve your listening by watching short clips without subtitles.
The panel comes off by pressing the two clips, not with a screwdriver.
grammar.watch: After “by”, always use -ing: “by checking”, never “by check” or “by to check”.
more: You can save fuel by flying lower.
We reduced costs by cutting travel.
By checking twice, we avoided the error.
She got the job by preparing three case studies.
You save time by not opening every message as it arrives.
They cut down on waste by ordering weekly instead of daily.

fix.wrong: We saved money by to buy in bulk.
fix.right: We saved money by buying in bulk.
fix.why: “By” is a preposition and takes a gerund.

fix.wrong: By don’t answering, you make it worse.
fix.right: By not answering, you make it worse.
fix.why: A gerund is negated with “not” before it.

fix.wrong: I opened it with pressing the button.
fix.right: I opened it by pressing the button.
fix.why: “By” names the method; “with” names the instrument.

drill.name: How, exactly
drill.prompt: Explain how to achieve each result with a “by + gerund” clause, then repeat it with the clause at the front.

dialogue.line: How did you cut the processing time?
By checking the data before we imported it.
That’s all?
That, and by not running the report twice. We were duplicating everything.

grammar.sound: “By” keeps its full diphthong and takes light stress, then the gerund carries the main stress: “by BOOKing early”.

speaking.text: Plan a trip with your partner. Every proposal must be stated with “would rather” or “would prefer”, and one of you must use “I’d rather you…” at least twice.
Explain how you achieved something — saved money, learned a skill, fixed a problem — in five steps, every step using “by + gerund”.
Your partner suggests five things you dislike. Decline each one with a different preference structure and a reason.

“I’d rather you didn’t” uses a past form for a present request.
After “by”, always -ing.

quiz.q: We reduced the error rate ___ every entry twice.
quiz.explain: “By” is a preposition of method and is always followed by a gerund: “by checking”.

dynamics.name: Impossible schedule
dynamics.how: Pairs receive a diary with clashing commitments and must negotiate a plan, stating every choice as a preference. Neither may simply agree; each must state an alternative.
dynamics.payoff: Real negotiation forces “would rather … than” rather than isolated sentences.

dynamics.name: Efficiency consultants
dynamics.how: Groups receive a wasteful process and must propose six improvements, each expressed as “by + gerund”, then present the two with the biggest saving.
dynamics.payoff: The method structure becomes the format of the whole presentation.

dynamics.name: I’d rather you didn’t
dynamics.how: Students write two requests they would make of a flatmate or colleague, phrased with “I’d rather you didn’t…”. Cards are read out and the class votes on which is most reasonable.
dynamics.payoff: Targets the past-form pattern, which learners rarely produce unprompted.

dynamics.name: Rather or prefer
dynamics.how: Teacher gives a pair of options; students must answer alternately with “rather” and “prefer”, keeping the structures correct at speed.
dynamics.payoff: Separates the two complement patterns before they fuse.

writing.title: How I’d do it differently
writing.brief: Describe a routine at work or at home that wastes time. State your preferences for how it should run, then explain the method for each improvement using “by + gerund”.
criteria: Four preference structures, including one “would rather + subject + past”.
Four “by + gerund” clauses, one of them negative and one at the front of its sentence.
No “prefer than” and no “rather to”.

homework.title: Preferences and methods
homework.task: Write six preferences about your week using both “would rather” and “would prefer”, then six sentences explaining how you achieved something, each with a “by + gerund” clause.

test.q: She’d prefer ___ the figures first.
test.explain: “Would prefer” takes “to + verb”.

test.explain: A preference about another person takes the past form.

test.explain: “By” takes a gerund to name the method.

test.explain: A gerund is negated with “not” before it.

units.title: REFIT
units.theme: Arranging for things to be done, and proposing ideas

overview.intro: You do not fix everything yourself. This sector covers the causative — get or have something done — which lets you say that you arranged a service rather than performed it, and then the full range of suggestion structures, from modals and gerunds to negative questions.
goals: Use get / have something done to describe arranged services.
Distinguish the causative from the ordinary passive and the active.
Make suggestions with modals, gerunds, negative questions and infinitives.
overview.outcome: By the end you can describe six things you had done rather than did, and lead a five-minute planning discussion using a different suggestion structure each time.

vocab.def: to arrange for someone else to do something for you.
vocab.use: “Get + object + past participle”: “I got my hair cut.” Slightly more informal than “have”.
examples: I need to get the brakes checked.
We got the whole flat repainted.
vocab.colloc: get it fixed · get your hair cut

vocab.def: the same idea, slightly more formal.
vocab.use: “Have + object + past participle”: “We had the roof repaired.” Also used for bad experiences: “She had her bag stolen.”
examples: We had the system upgraded last month.
He had his licence suspended.
vocab.colloc: have it serviced · have it delivered

vocab.def: to check and maintain a machine or vehicle.
vocab.use: Transitive: “service the engine”. Noun: “a service”, “due for a service”.
examples: The van is being serviced today.
We have it serviced twice a year.
vocab.colloc: have it serviced · a full service

vocab.def: a stated price for a job before it is done.
vocab.use: “Get a quote”, “ask for an estimate”. A quote is usually fixed; an estimate is approximate.
examples: I got three quotes for the repair.
Their estimate was twice as high.
vocab.colloc: get a quote · a rough estimate

vocab.def: to put equipment or software in place so it works.
vocab.use: Transitive: “install a new panel”. Noun: installation.
examples: We had solar panels installed.
The software is being installed remotely.
vocab.colloc: have it installed · installation costs

vocab.def: a suggestion opener followed by -ing or a noun.
vocab.use: “How about meeting at six?” Never followed by an infinitive.
examples: How about starting an hour earlier?
How about Friday instead?
vocab.colloc: how about tomorrow · what about you

vocab.def: a friendly suggestion followed by a base verb.
vocab.use: “Why don’t we ask them first?” The answer is usually “good idea” or a counter-proposal.
examples: Why don’t we split the task?
Why don’t you ask your supervisor?
vocab.colloc: why don’t we · why not try

vocab.def: good enough to attempt.
vocab.use: “It’s worth a try” or “it’s worth trying”. Never an infinitive.
examples: It’s worth a try, at least.
That’s worth trying before we call support.
vocab.colloc: well worth a try · worth trying

vocab.term: to talk someone into / out of
vocab.def: to persuade someone to do / not to do something.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or -ing: “talked me into buying it”, “talked her out of resigning”.
examples: She talked me into getting it repaired instead.
I talked him out of doing it himself.
vocab.colloc: talk someone into it · talk yourself out of

vocab.def: to proceed with a plan.
vocab.use: Intransitive, often with “with”: “go ahead with the repair”. Also a permission phrase: “Go ahead.”
examples: We decided to go ahead with the upgrade.
Shall I book it? — Go ahead.
vocab.colloc: go ahead with the plan · give the go-ahead

vocab.def: to finally do something you have been meaning to do.
vocab.use: Three-part and followed by a noun or -ing: “I still haven’t got round to fixing it.”
examples: I never got round to calling them back.
We’ll get round to the paperwork tomorrow.
vocab.colloc: get round to it · never got round to · finally got round to

vocab.def: good enough as an idea to attempt, even if it may not work.
vocab.use: Closes a suggestion: “It might not help, but it’s worth a try.”
examples: It’s a long shot, but it’s worth a try.
Restarting it is always worth a try.
vocab.colloc: worth a try · worth a shot · definitely worth a try

grammar.name: Get or have something done
grammar.short: I had the engine serviced. / We’re getting the panel replaced.
grammar.rule: The causative says that you arranged for someone else to do the work. The structure is “have” or “get” plus the object plus a past participle. The person who did the job is normally left out entirely.
form: have + object + past participle → We had the roof repaired.
get + object + past participle → I’m getting my laptop fixed.
All tenses on have/get: I’ve had it serviced. / I’ll get it checked. / I was having it repaired.
Question / negative: Did you have it delivered? / We haven’t had it inspected yet.
Naming the worker (rare): We had a technician check the wiring. (active: no participle)
notes: Compare three sentences: “I repaired the car” (I did it), “I had the car repaired” (someone did it for me), “The car was repaired” (passive, no mention of arrangement).
“Get” is slightly more informal and often implies more effort or persuasion; “have” is neutral.
With “have + person + base verb” the worker is named and the verb is active: “I had the plumber look at it.”
The causative also reports things done to you that you did not want: “She had her bag stolen.”
Do not use an infinitive: “I had the car to repair” means something completely different.
grammar.deep: The causative exists because English needs to distinguish doing from arranging, and most languages mark that difference with a separate verb. “I cut my hair” means you held the scissors; “I had my hair cut” means you sat in a chair while somebody else did. That distinction matters more than it looks, because at B1 learners routinely claim to have rewired their own flat or serviced their own car. The structure is mechanically simple — object first, participle second — and the tense is carried entirely by “have” or “get”, so all the usual forms are available. Two extras are worth knowing. “Have + person + base verb” names the worker and switches to an active infinitive, which is useful when the person matters. And the same structure reports misfortune, so “he had his licence suspended” arranges nothing at all — context tells your listener which reading applies.

chart.title: Who did the work?
rows: I had a decorator paint it.

examples: We’re having the navigation system upgraded next week.
I got my documents translated because I couldn’t do it myself.
Have you had the brakes checked since the trip?
They had their contract cancelled without any warning.
grammar.watch: Use a past participle, not an infinitive: “I had it repaired”, never “I had it to repair”.
more: We’re having the navigation system upgraded next week.
I got my documents translated because I couldn’t do it myself.
Have you had the brakes checked since the trip?
They had the whole office repainted over the weekend.
She’s getting her contract reviewed before she signs.
We had two panels replaced and the third one repaired.

fix.wrong: I had it to repair.
fix.right: I had it repaired.
fix.why: The causative takes a past participle, not an infinitive.

fix.wrong: I had repaired my car last week.
fix.right: I had my car repaired last week.
fix.why: Word order decides the meaning: object first, then participle.

fix.wrong: We are going to have upgraded the system.
fix.right: We are going to have the system upgraded.
fix.why: The object must sit between “have” and the participle.

drill.name: Did you do it yourself?
drill.prompt: Say each sentence twice: once as something you did, once as something you arranged. Keep the tense the same.

dialogue.line: Did you repaint the flat yourself?
No, we had it done while we were away.
And the floors?
We’re getting those sanded next month. I’d rather not do that one myself.

contrast.title: Who did the work
rows: I got him to sign it.

grammar.sound: In “I had it repaired” the stress falls on the participle, and “had it” collapses to /hædɪt/. Stressing “had” turns it into the past perfect auxiliary by mistake.

grammar.name: Making suggestions with modals, gerunds, negative questions and infinitives
grammar.short: We could ask. How about asking? Why don’t we ask? It might be worth asking.
grammar.rule: English has a graded set of suggestion structures. Modals propose an option, gerund frames propose an activity, negative questions invite agreement, and infinitive frames make the suggestion impersonal.
form: Modal: We could / should / might ask them first.
Gerund frames: How about asking them? / What about a different supplier?
Negative question: Why don’t we ask them? / Couldn’t we ask them?
Infinitive frame: It might be better to ask them. / The best thing to do is to ask.
Shared action: Let’s ask them. / Shall we ask them?
notes: “How about” and “What about” take a gerund or a noun, never an infinitive: “How about meeting?”, not “How about to meet”.
“Why don’t we” takes a base verb: “Why don’t we start now?”
Negative questions expect agreement, which makes them softer than a bare imperative but stronger than “could”.
“Suggest” and “recommend” never take an object plus infinitive: say “I suggest asking” or “I suggest that we ask”, never “I suggest us to ask”.
“Shall we…?” is a genuine invitation to decide together, and it is more common in British English.
grammar.deep: Suggestions are the same content at different social temperatures, and choosing the temperature is the real skill. “We could ask them” offers an option and leaves the decision open. “Why don’t we ask them?” presents your idea as the obvious next step and invites agreement, so it is warmer but more directive. “It might be better to ask them” removes you from the sentence entirely, turning the suggestion into a general observation — the safest form when you are contradicting someone senior. In a meeting, moving through these forms keeps you from sounding either passive or pushy. Two mechanics protect the structures: gerunds after “how about” and “what about”, base verbs after “why don’t”. And remember that “suggest” resists the object-plus-infinitive pattern, which is one of the most persistent errors carried up from A2.

chart.title: Suggestion structures by temperature
rows: It might be better to postpone.

examples: How about getting a second quote before we decide?
Why don’t we have it serviced while the bay is free?
It might be better to replace the whole unit than to keep repairing it.
Couldn’t we ask the supplier to send a technician?
grammar.watch: “How about” takes -ing, “why don’t we” takes a base verb, and “I suggest” never takes “us to”.
more: We could ask them before we order anything.
How about asking the supplier for a sample?
Why don’t we run the test twice?
It might be worth asking a second opinion.
What about a shorter meeting instead?
Couldn’t we just postpone it a week?

fix.wrong: How about to ask them?
fix.right: How about asking them?
fix.why: “How about” and “what about” take a gerund or a noun.

fix.wrong: Why we don’t ask them?
fix.right: Why don’t we ask them?
fix.why: The negative question keeps standard inversion.

fix.wrong: It might be worth to ask.
fix.right: It might be worth asking.
fix.why: “Worth” is always followed by a gerund.

drill.name: Five ways to suggest
drill.prompt: Propose one solution to each problem five times, using a modal, a gerund frame, a negative question, an infinitive frame and “let’s”.
items: the team never meets in person

dialogue.line: The rollout keeps slipping.
How about freezing the scope for two weeks?
We could, but the client won’t like it.
Why don’t we show them the numbers first? It might be worth trying.

grammar.sound: A suggestion rises at the end and stresses the new idea: “How about ASKing them?” A falling tone on the same words turns it into a complaint.

speaking.kind: Did you or did you have it done?
speaking.text: List eight things that happened to your home, car or devices last year. Your partner asks whether you did each one or had it done.
Plan an event in five minutes. Every contribution must use a different suggestion structure, and nobody may repeat one.
Try to talk your partner into a plan they dislike, escalating from “we could” to “why don’t we” to “it might be better to”.

tips: Causative = have/get + object + past participle.
“How about” + -ing; “why don’t we” + base verb.
“I suggest asking” or “I suggest that we ask” — never “I suggest us to ask”.

quiz.q: We’re going to ___ the whole system ___ next month.
quiz.explain: The causative takes an object followed by a past participle: “have the system upgraded”.

dynamics.name: Service directory
dynamics.how: Each pair lists eight things they had done in the last year and eight they did themselves, then quizzes another pair, who must guess which is which from the structure alone.
dynamics.payoff: The causative is only detectable through form, so it must be accurate.

dynamics.name: Problem clinic
dynamics.how: Each student brings a real problem. The group must produce five suggestions per problem, each with a different frame, and the owner chooses one and says why.
dynamics.payoff: Five frames per problem prevents the class defaulting to “you should”.

dynamics.name: Renovation budget
dynamics.how: Groups plan a renovation with a fixed budget, deciding what to do themselves and what to have done, and present the plan with the costs.
dynamics.payoff: The two structures contrast inside a single decision.

dynamics.name: Suggestion tennis
dynamics.how: A makes a suggestion, B rejects it with a reason and makes another. Neither may repeat a frame. Ten exchanges.
dynamics.payoff: Speed plus the no-repeat rule drives the rarer frames out.

writing.title: The refit plan
writing.brief: Describe a renovation, repair project or upgrade. Say what you had or will have done by someone else, using the causative, and propose three further improvements using three different suggestion frames.
criteria: Four causative structures with the object before the participle.
Three different suggestion frames, correctly complemented.
At least one “get + object + participle”.

homework.title: Had it done
homework.task: Write eight sentences about services you arranged in the last year, using have and get in different tenses. Then write five suggestions for improving something at work, each with a different frame.

test.q: We’re going to ___ the whole system ___ next month.
test.explain: The causative is have + object + past participle.

test.q: I ___ my documents translated last week.
test.explain: “Get” works exactly like “have” in the causative.

test.q: How about ___ the supplier first?
test.explain: “How about” takes a gerund.

test.q: ___ we run the test twice?
test.explain: The negative question keeps normal inversion.

test.q: It might be worth ___ a second opinion.
test.explain: “Worth” takes a gerund.

Beneath it two contrasting sentences: I repaired the door. / I had the door repaired.
A small note: get = have, just less formal.

units.title: TRAJECTORY
units.theme: Predicting what lies ahead and locating what lies behind

overview.intro: Navigation runs in both directions. This sector gives you three future forms for prediction — will, the future continuous and the future perfect — and then the whole set of adverbs and prepositions for placing an event accurately in the past.
goals: Predict with will, the future continuous and the future perfect.
Choose the right future form for a moment, an ongoing action and a completed one.
Refer to past time precisely with during, in, ago, from…to, for and since.
overview.outcome: By the end you can describe your life five years from now in three future forms, and give a precise timeline of the last five years.

vocab.def: probable.
vocab.use: “Be likely to + verb” or “It’s likely that…”. Opposite: “unlikely”.
examples: Prices are likely to rise next year.
She’s unlikely to accept the offer.
vocab.colloc: highly likely · likely outcome

vocab.def: before or at that future moment.
vocab.use: Strong triggers for the future perfect: “By then we’ll have finished.”
examples: By then I’ll have graduated.
By that time the system will have been replaced.
vocab.colloc: by then · by the end of the year

vocab.def: for now, until the situation changes.
vocab.use: Usually at the start or the end: “For the time being, we’re staying put.”
examples: For the time being, nothing changes.
We’ll use the old version for the time being.
vocab.colloc: for the time being · for now

vocab.def: at some point within a period of time.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun, never a clause: “during the meeting”, not “during it rained”.
examples: It happened during the night shift.
I studied abroad during my second year.
vocab.colloc: during the summer · during the meeting

vocab.def: before now, counting backwards.
vocab.use: Always after the time period, and always with the simple past: “two years ago”.
examples: I met her three months ago.
We moved here a long time ago.
vocab.colloc: a while ago · not long ago

vocab.def: marking a start point and an end point.
vocab.use: “From 2019 to 2022”. In American English “from Monday through Friday” includes Friday.
examples: I worked there from 2018 to 2021.
The bay is closed from nine to five.
vocab.colloc: from Monday to Friday · from start to finish

vocab.def: an important point in a plan or a life.
vocab.use: Countable: “reach a milestone”. Common in goal-setting.
examples: The next milestone is the pressure test.
It was a real milestone for the team.
vocab.colloc: reach a milestone · a major milestone

vocab.def: to think about the future.
vocab.use: Intransitive, often with “to”: “looking ahead to next year”.
examples: Looking ahead, I’d like to specialise.
Let’s look ahead to the next phase.
vocab.colloc: look ahead to · looking further ahead

vocab.def: in the end, after some time.
vocab.use: Not the same as “possibly”. Useful in future narratives: “Eventually we’ll automate it.”
examples: Eventually they’ll replace the whole fleet.
She eventually agreed.
vocab.colloc: eventually happen · eventually replaced

vocab.def: progressing as planned.
vocab.use: With “be”, often with “to + verb” or “for + noun”: “on track to finish by June”.
examples: We’re on track to finish ahead of schedule.
The project is back on track.
vocab.colloc: on track to finish · back on track

vocab.def: before or at that future or past point.
vocab.use: Pairs naturally with the perfect: “By then we’ll have finished.”
examples: The permits arrive in May; by then we’ll have started.
By then it was too late to change anything.
vocab.colloc: by then · by that time · long before then

grammar.name: Predicting the future with will, the future continuous and the future perfect
grammar.short: I’ll be working. / By June I’ll have finished.
grammar.rule: Three forms describe three shapes of future. “Will” states a prediction or a decision. The future continuous describes an action in progress at a future moment. The future perfect describes an action completed before a future deadline.
form: will + base verb → Prices will rise next year.
will be + -ing → At ten tomorrow I’ll be flying.
will have + past participle → By December I’ll have finished the course.
will have been + -ing (duration) → By May I’ll have been working here a year.
Negative / question: won’t be working · Will you have finished by then?
notes: Time markers do most of the work: “at ten tomorrow” pulls the continuous, “by December” pulls the perfect.
The future continuous is also a polite way of asking about plans without sounding like a request: “Will you be using the car tonight?”
After “by the time”, the verb stays in the present: “By the time you arrive, we’ll have started.”
State verbs stay simple: “I’ll have known her for ten years”, not “will have been knowing”.
“Going to” remains the form for a plan already decided; these three are for prediction and projection.
grammar.deep: Once you have more than one future form, the time expression usually chooses for you. A point in time — “at nine tomorrow”, “this time next week” — asks what will be in progress then, so it takes the continuous. A deadline — “by Friday”, “by the end of the quarter” — asks what will be complete before it, so it takes the perfect. Bare “will” has no shape at all, which is why it suits general predictions and instant decisions. The future perfect is the form most learners avoid and the one that most raises the level of a plan, because it lets you look back from a point you have not reached yet: “by the time the audit starts, we’ll have replaced both units.” Note the recurring rule about time clauses — no future form after “by the time”, “when” or “as soon as” — which applies here exactly as it did in sector 08.

chart.title: Which future form?
rows: at nine tomorrow, this time next week
by Friday, by then, by the end of…
I’ll have been working here a year.

examples: This time next month I’ll be working in a different department.
By the end of the year we’ll have replaced every unit in the fleet.
I don’t think prices will fall, but they probably won’t rise much either.
Will you be using the simulator this afternoon? I need an hour on it.
grammar.watch: No future form after “by the time”: “By the time you arrive, we’ll have started”, not “will arrive”.
more: This time next month I’ll be working in a different department.
By December we’ll have replaced every unit in the fleet.
I don’t think prices will fall, but they probably won’t rise much either.
At ten tomorrow they’ll be presenting to the board.
By the time you land, we’ll have finished the setup.
She’ll have been with the company ten years in March.

fix.wrong: By the time you will arrive, we’ll have started.
fix.right: By the time you arrive, we’ll have started.
fix.why: A time clause never takes a future form.

fix.wrong: At ten tomorrow I will work.
fix.right: At ten tomorrow I’ll be working.
fix.why: An action in progress at a future moment takes the future continuous.

fix.wrong: By June I will finish the course.
fix.right: By June I’ll have finished the course.
fix.why: Completion before a deadline takes the future perfect.

drill.name: Three futures
drill.prompt: For each moment, produce a prediction with will, an action in progress with the future continuous, and a completed result with the future perfect.
items: by the end of the month
by the time you get back

dialogue.line: Will the fleet be ready for the inspection?
By then we’ll have replaced every unit.
And the paperwork?

rows: in progress at a future point
duration up to a future point
By May I’ll have been studying two years.

grammar.sound: “Will have” contracts twice in speech — “I’ll’ve finished” /aɪləv/ — so the whole future perfect can sound like a single syllable before the participle.

grammar.name: Referring to time in the past: during, in, ago, from…to, for, since
grammar.short: during the summer · in 2019 · two years ago · for six months · since March
grammar.rule: Each of these expressions locates a past event differently: some name a period, some a point, some a duration, and some a starting point. Their grammar is fixed, and the tense they take is part of the pattern.
form: during + noun (period) → It happened during the night.
in + month / year / season → We met in 2019.
on + day / date → We signed on 3 May.
ago + simple past → I left two years ago.
from … to … → I worked there from 2018 to 2021.
for + duration → I worked there for three years.
since + starting point + present perfect → I’ve worked here since March.
notes: “During” takes a noun; for a clause use “while”: “during the flight” but “while we were flying”.
“Ago” goes after the period and only with the simple past — never with the present perfect.
“For” answers “how long?” and works with several tenses; “since” gives a starting point and normally requires the present perfect.
“From … to …” marks a closed period, so it takes the simple past: “from 2018 to 2021 I worked…”.
“In” is also used for a future interval: “in two weeks” means two weeks from now, not two weeks ago.
grammar.deep: Time reference is where accurate B1 writing is won or lost, because these words are fixed and a wrong one is noticed immediately. Group them by what they measure. “During”, “in” and “on” locate an event inside a period, in decreasing size. “Ago” and “from … to …” both describe closed time and therefore both take the simple past. “For” measures duration and can appear with almost any tense, while “since” names a starting point and pulls the present perfect with it, because a starting point implies the situation continues. The pair that causes most trouble is “for” and “since”, and the fix is to look at what follows rather than at the meaning: a length of time takes “for”, a point on the calendar takes “since”. Note also that “ago” and “since” are mutually exclusive — “since two years ago” is a mix of two systems.

chart.title: Past time expressions
rows: I lived there for two years.

examples: I worked in the maintenance division from 2017 to 2020, and I’ve been in operations since then.
The fault appeared during the second test, about ten minutes ago.
We’ve had the same equipment for six years, and nothing has failed since the upgrade.
In March we replaced the sensors; on 12 April the whole unit failed anyway.
grammar.watch: “For” + duration, “since” + starting point, and never “since two years ago”.
more: It happened during the night, some time before three.
We met in 2019 and worked together for two years.
I left the company two years ago.
She’s been in the role since March.
The contract ran from January to September.
We haven’t spoken since the conference.

fix.right: I’ve worked here since 2019.
fix.why: “Since” with a period up to now requires a perfect tense.

fix.right: for three hours

fix.right: I left two years ago.

drill.name: Place it in time
drill.prompt: Describe each event three times, using a different time expression each time, and adjust the tense to match.
items: the last time you moved house

dialogue.line: How long have you been in maintenance?
Since 2019 — about seven years.
And before that?
I worked in logistics for three years, and I left just before the merger.

grammar.sound: “For” is reduced to /fə/ before a consonant and “since” keeps its /s/ clearly. In fast speech “for” almost disappears, so the number after it must be clear.

speaking.text: Describe your life five years from now in six sentences: two with will, two with the future continuous, two with the future perfect.
Give a precise five-year timeline of your studies or career, using during, in, ago, from…to, for and since at least once each.
In pairs, predict three changes in your field. For each one say what will be happening and what will have happened by a stated deadline.

“Ago” only with the simple past; “since” only with the perfect.
No future form after “by the time”.

quiz.explain: An action completed before a future deadline takes the future perfect, and “by the time” keeps its own clause in the present.

dynamics.payoff: Both future forms are needed by the frame itself.

dynamics.name: Timeline interview
dynamics.how: Students draw a personal timeline with six points and interview each other about it, using a different time expression in every question.
dynamics.payoff: Puts the whole expression set into questions, not just answers.

dynamics.name: For or since

dynamics.payoff: Fast correction of the highest-frequency error in the node.

writing.title: Where this is heading

No future form inside a time clause.
Four different past time expressions with the tense each requires.

units.title: REROUTE
units.theme: Sequencing events, and regretting the route you took

overview.intro: Two structures that both depend on control of time. Time clauses order events precisely — before, after, once, the moment, as soon as, until, by the time — and then the unreal past lets you regret a decision and imagine the journey you did not take.
goals: Use time clauses with the correct tense in past, present and future reference.
Express regret with should (not) have + past participle.
Build third conditional sentences with if + past perfect and would/could have + past participle.
overview.outcome: By the end you can narrate a sequence of events with five different time conjunctions, and review a past decision with regret and a hypothetical alternative.

vocab.def: immediately when; as soon as.
vocab.use: Works as a conjunction: “Call me the moment you land.” Also “the minute”, “the second”.
examples: The moment I saw the reading, I knew.
Let me know the moment it arrives.
vocab.colloc: the moment you arrive · the minute I saw it

vocab.def: as soon as; after something has happened.
vocab.use: Followed by a clause with a present or past tense, never a future: “once we know”.
examples: Once the checks are complete, we can launch.
Once I’d read the report, everything made sense.
vocab.colloc: once we know · once it’s finished

vocab.def: up to the moment when.
vocab.use: Marks an end point, not a duration. With a negative it means “not before”: “Don’t leave until I call.”
examples: We waited until the storm passed.
I won’t decide until I speak to her.
vocab.colloc: until now · not until · up until then

vocab.def: to feel sorry about something you did or did not do.
vocab.use: “Regret + -ing” for the past action: “I regret sending it.” “Regret to inform” is a formal announcement.
examples: I regret not taking that offer.
She regrets telling him.
vocab.colloc: deeply regret · no regrets

vocab.def: to refuse an offer.
vocab.use: Separable: “turn down the offer”, “turn it down”. Also “reduce the volume”.
examples: I turned down the job and I still think about it.
They turned our proposal down.
vocab.colloc: turn down an offer · turn it down

vocab.def: looking back with what you know now.
vocab.use: Usually opens the sentence and pairs with past modals: “In hindsight, I should have waited.”
examples: In hindsight, the signs were obvious.
With hindsight, we moved too fast.
vocab.colloc: in hindsight · with the benefit of hindsight

vocab.def: to say someone is responsible for something bad.
vocab.use: “Blame someone for something”. “To be to blame” = to be responsible.
examples: Don’t blame me for the delay.
Nobody was to blame.
vocab.colloc: take the blame · who’s to blame

vocab.def: if not; in the other case.
vocab.use: Links a condition to a consequence across two clauses: “Write it down; otherwise you’ll forget.”
examples: Leave now, otherwise you’ll miss it.
She apologised; otherwise I’d have complained.
vocab.colloc: otherwise fine · or otherwise

vocab.def: something you learn from an experience.
vocab.use: “Learn a lesson”, “an expensive lesson”. Useful for closing a regret story.
examples: It was an expensive lesson.
I learnt my lesson that day.
vocab.colloc: a hard lesson · learn your lesson

vocab.def: in place of.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or -ing: “instead of waiting”. Never an infinitive.
examples: I should have called instead of sending an email.
Instead of complaining, we rebuilt it.
vocab.colloc: instead of that · rather than

vocab.def: to fail to happen after being planned.
vocab.use: Intransitive, used of plans and deals: “The deal fell through at the last minute.”
examples: The trip fell through because of the strike.
Two of the three offers fell through.
vocab.colloc: the deal fell through · plans fell through

vocab.def: judging with knowledge you did not have at the time.
vocab.use: Opens a regret and pairs with “should have” or a third conditional.
examples: With hindsight, we moved too fast.
It was the wrong route, with hindsight.
vocab.colloc: with hindsight · in hindsight · hindsight is a fine thing

grammar.name: Time clauses: before, after, once, the moment, as soon as, until, by the time
grammar.short: As soon as I finish, I’ll call you.
grammar.rule: A time clause says when the main action happens. It can come first or second; if it comes first, it takes a comma. English never puts a future form inside a time clause — the future lives only in the main clause.
form: Future reference: As soon as I finish, I’ll send it. (present simple in the clause)
Stressing completion: Once I’ve finished, I’ll send it. (present perfect)
Past sequence: After I sent it, she called.
Earlier past event: By the time we arrived, it had closed.
Reduced with -ing (same subject): Before leaving, check the lights.
notes: This is the rule examiners look for: “when I will arrive” is always wrong. Use the present simple.
“Until” marks an end point and often appears with a negative main clause: “I won’t decide until I hear from them.”
“By the time” usually pulls the past perfect in past narration and the future perfect in future reference.
“As soon as”, “the moment” and “once” all mean there is no gap between the two events; “after” allows one.
A reduced -ing clause is only possible when both clauses share the same subject.
grammar.deep: Time clauses look easy and then quietly break sentences, because they run on a rule that feels illogical: the clause refers to the future but its verb is in the present. The reason is that English marks the future only once. The main clause carries “will” or “going to”, and the conjunction — when, once, as soon as, until — already tells you where you are, so the subordinate clause does not repeat the marking. Spanish uses a subjunctive in exactly this slot, which is why the error is so persistent. The second skill is conjunction choice, because it encodes your reading of events: “when the alarm sounded, we left” (sequence), “as soon as the alarm sounded, we left” (immediately), “once the alarm had sounded, we left” (after completion), “we waited until the alarm sounded” (end point). Same facts, four different stories.

chart.title: Tense inside time clauses
rows: present simple: as soon as I finish
present: by the time you arrive
past simple: after I sent it
