examples: I’ll forward the report as soon as I’ve checked the figures.
Once the tests are complete, the bay will be reopened.
By the time the engineers got there, the leak had already stopped.
We won’t change anything until we understand what caused it.
grammar.watch: Never put “will” in a time clause: “when I arrive”, not “when I will arrive”.
more: I’ll forward the report as soon as I’ve checked the figures.
Once the tests are complete, the bay will be reopened.
By the time the engineers got there, the leak had stopped.
We can’t start until the permit arrives.
The moment she signs it, I’ll send you a copy.
After we had reviewed the log, the pattern was obvious.

fix.wrong: I’ll call you when I will arrive.
fix.right: I’ll call you when I arrive.
fix.why: A time clause takes a present form even for future meaning.

fix.wrong: Until you won’t confirm, we can’t book.
fix.right: Until you confirm, we can’t book.
fix.why: “Until” is already negative in force and takes no extra negative.

fix.wrong: After I finished, I had gone home.
fix.right: After I had finished, I went home.
fix.why: The past perfect marks the earlier event, not the later one.

drill.name: Order the sequence
drill.prompt: Join each pair of events with a different time conjunction, keeping the tenses correct, then reverse the order of the clauses.
items: she signs / I send the copy
we check the figures / we publish
the shift ends / the report is filed
the parts land / the line restarts

dialogue.line: When can we restart the line?
As soon as the parts clear customs.
And the paperwork?
Once I’ve signed it off, you can go ahead. By the time you’re ready, it’ll be done.

grammar.sound: The time clause is spoken as one unstressed run, with the stress reserved for the main clause: “as soon as I finish, I’ll CALL you.”

grammar.name: Regret with should (not) have; hypothetical past with if + past perfect
grammar.short: I should have checked. / If I had checked, this wouldn’t have happened.
grammar.rule: To comment on a past you cannot change, English adds “have + past participle” to a modal. “Should have” expresses regret or criticism. The third conditional puts an unreal past condition with the past perfect and an unreal past result with would/could/might have + participle.
form: Regret: I should have booked earlier. (I didn’t.)
Criticism: You shouldn’t have said that. (You did.)
Third conditional: If I had checked the log, I would have seen the error.
Other results: could have (possibility) · might have (uncertain outcome).
Reversed order, no comma: I would have seen the error if I had checked the log.
notes: The pattern is always modal + have + participle: never “should had” and never “should of”, which is a spelling of the spoken “should’ve”.
“Should have” criticises the past; “should” alone advises the present: “You should call her” versus “You should have called her”.
No “would” in the if-clause: “If I would have known” is wrong. The condition takes the past perfect.
“Could have” has two meanings — an unrealised possibility (“we could have won”) and a past deduction (“she could have forgotten”).
In speech these all contract heavily: should’ve, would’ve, could’ve, hadn’t. Train your ear for them.
grammar.deep: The unreal past is one step further back than the unreal present, and that extra step is what makes it impossible to change. “If I had time, I would help” imagines a different now; “if I had had time, I would have helped” imagines a different then, and no action can alter it. That is why the third conditional is the grammar of post-mortems, and why it pairs so naturally with “should have”. The two structures say related things with different emphasis: “I should have checked” admits fault, while “if I had checked, this wouldn’t have happened” traces the consequence. Two traps recur at B1. “Would” never appears in the if-clause — the condition is marked by the past perfect alone. And the written form is “should have” or “should’ve”; “should of” appears only because the spoken contraction sounds like it, and it is always wrong on paper.

chart.title: Regret and the third conditional
rows: If I had known, I would have called.
If we hadn’t left late, we wouldn’t have missed it.

examples: I should have run the diagnostics before signing off on the repair.
You shouldn’t have paid in cash — now there’s no record.
If we had ordered the part in March, it would have arrived before the refit.
They could have avoided the whole delay if somebody had read the manual.
grammar.watch: Write “should have” or “should’ve”, never “should of”, and keep “would” out of the if-clause.
more: I should have checked the log before I reported it.
You shouldn’t have signed without reading it.
If I had checked, this wouldn’t have happened.
If they had told us earlier, we could have rescheduled.
We would have caught it if the alarm had worked.
With hindsight, I should have asked for it in writing.

fix.wrong: If I would have known, I would have told you.
fix.right: If I had known, I would have told you.
fix.why: “Would” never appears in the if-clause.

fix.wrong: I should of checked.
fix.right: I should have checked.
fix.why: “Should of” is a spelling of the reduced sound, not a structure.

fix.wrong: If I had checked, this wouldn’t happen.
fix.right: If I had checked, this wouldn’t have happened.
fix.why: An unreal past result needs “have + participle” too.

drill.name: Rewind the decision
drill.prompt: For each situation, state the regret with “should have” and then the unreal outcome with a full third conditional.

dialogue.line: The whole order went to the wrong depot.
We should have confirmed the address.
Would it have arrived on time?
If we’d called on Monday, it would have been there by Wednesday.

grammar.sound: Both halves contract heavily: “If I’d known, I would’ve told you” /ɪfaɪd … wʊdəv/. The tense lives entirely in the participles.

speaking.text: Build a group story where each student adds one sentence beginning with a different time conjunction: before, after, once, the moment, as soon as, until, by the time.
Review a plan that went wrong. Each person contributes one “should have”, one “could have” and one full third conditional.
Choose one decision from your past and describe three consequences that would have followed if you had chosen differently.

tips: Time clause = present tense, even for the future.
Modal + have + participle. Never “should of”.
The if-clause of a third conditional takes the past perfect, never “would”.

quiz.q: If we ___ the part earlier, it would have arrived on time.
quiz.explain: A third conditional takes the past perfect in the if-clause and “would have + participle” in the result.

dynamics.name: Project post-mortem
dynamics.how: Groups read a one-page account of a failed project, list six things that should have happened, then write four third conditionals describing how it would have ended differently.
dynamics.payoff: Both structures are the natural response to the material.

dynamics.name: Sequence cards
dynamics.how: Groups receive eight event cards and must narrate the sequence using a different time conjunction for each join, out loud, with no repeats.
dynamics.payoff: The no-repeat rule forces the whole conjunction set into use.

dynamics.name: Regret auction
dynamics.how: Students write one anonymous regret with “should have”. Cards are read out; the class votes on which was the most avoidable and rewrites it as a third conditional.
dynamics.payoff: Links the two structures explicitly.

dynamics.name: Never will in a time clause
dynamics.how: Teacher dictates ten sentences at speed, half containing an error; students hold up a card each time they hear “will” inside a time clause.
dynamics.payoff: Trains the ear on the error rather than the page.

writing.title: What went wrong and when
writing.brief: Narrate something that did not go to plan. Part one: the sequence of events, joined with at least four different time conjunctions. Part two: what should have happened, and what would have happened if it had.
criteria: Four different time conjunctions, none containing a future form.
Three past modals of regret or criticism.
Two complete third conditionals with correct halves.

homework.title: Sequence and regret
homework.task: Write eight sentences about next week using time clauses, checking that none contains “will”. Then write six third conditionals about last month, underlining the past perfect in each if-clause.

test.q: If we ___ the part earlier, it would have arrived on time.
test.explain: The third conditional takes the past perfect in the if-clause.

test.q: I’ll call you as soon as I ___ .
test.explain: A time clause takes the present simple for future meaning.

test.q: You ___ signed it without reading it.
test.explain: The structure is modal + have + past participle.

test.q: We can’t start ___ the permit arrives.
test.explain: “Until” marks the point up to which something does not happen.

test.q: If the alarm had worked, we ___ it earlier.
test.explain: An unreal past result takes would have + participle.

units.title: MANIFEST
units.theme: Saying what something is for and why it happened

overview.intro: Every entry on a manifest answers two questions: what is it for, and why is it here. This sector gives you purpose — infinitive clauses, including the version with “for” when the purpose belongs to somebody else — and the full inventory of reason connectors, each with its own grammar.
goals: Express purpose with infinitive clauses and with for + object + infinitive.
Distinguish purpose (why) from function (what for).
Give reasons with because, since, because of, for, due to and the reason.
overview.outcome: By the end you can explain the purpose of six objects or decisions and justify each one with a different reason connector.

vocab.def: the reason why something exists or is done.
vocab.use: “The purpose of X is to + verb”. “On purpose” means deliberately — a different meaning.
examples: The purpose of the checklist is to catch small errors.
He did it on purpose.
vocab.colloc: the main purpose · serve a purpose

vocab.def: designed for a particular use or group.
vocab.use: Passive with “for + noun” or “to + verb”: “intended for professional use”.
examples: This tool is intended for heavy-duty work.
The guide is intended to help newcomers.
vocab.colloc: intended for use in · intended audience

vocab.def: because of.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or -ing, never a clause: “due to a fault”.
examples: The delay was due to a technical fault.
Due to demand, we added a session.
vocab.colloc: due to bad weather · largely due to

vocab.def: a slightly more formal “because of”.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun: “owing to heavy rain”. Common in announcements.
examples: Owing to the storm, all flights were grounded.
Owing to staff shortages, the desk is closed.
vocab.colloc: owing to circumstances

vocab.def: the explanation for something.
vocab.use: “The reason why X is that…” or “the reason for + noun”. Note “is that”, not “is because”.
examples: The reason why I called is that nobody answered the email.
The reason for the delay is unclear.
vocab.colloc: the main reason why · for that reason

vocab.def: to give good reasons for something.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or -ing: “justify the cost”, “justify spending more”. Never an infinitive.
examples: The results justify the extra expense.
How do you justify raising the price?
vocab.colloc: hard to justify · justify a decision

vocab.def: the underlying reason for a decision.
vocab.use: Formal, countable: “the rationale behind the change”.
examples: Nobody explained the rationale behind the new rule.
The rationale is purely financial.
vocab.colloc: the rationale behind · a clear rationale

vocab.def: in order that — followed by a clause.
vocab.use: Use it when the purpose has a different subject or needs a modal: “so that everyone can see”.
examples: We moved the briefing so that the night crew could attend.
Label it so that nobody uses the wrong one.
vocab.colloc: so that everyone can · so as to

vocab.def: to prevent or stay away from something.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or -ing, never an infinitive: “avoid making mistakes”.
examples: We left early to avoid the traffic.
Avoid clicking unknown links.
vocab.colloc: avoid a problem · hard to avoid

vocab.def: and as a result of that (formal).
vocab.use: Followed by -ing in written English: “thereby reducing costs”. Rare in speech.
examples: We automated the checks, thereby cutting the time in half.
It failed, thereby delaying everything.
vocab.colloc: thereby reducing · thereby avoiding

vocab.def: to explain the reason for something, or to make up a proportion of it.
vocab.use: Inseparable: “That accounts for the delay.” Also used with figures: “Freight accounts for 30% of costs.”
examples: The storm accounts for most of the damage.
Two suppliers account for half the total spend.
vocab.colloc: account for the delay · that accounts for it

grammar.name: Describing purpose with infinitive clauses and with for
grammar.short: We stopped to refuel. / We stopped for the crew to rest.
grammar.rule: Purpose answers “why?”. The default form is “to + verb”, raised in register by “in order to” and “so as to”. When the purpose belongs to a different subject, English uses “for + object + infinitive”, or a clause with “so that”.
form: to + verb → I called to confirm the booking.
in order to / so as to + verb → We left early in order to avoid the traffic.
Negative: in order not to / so as not to → I whispered so as not to wake her.
for + object + infinitive → We stopped for the crew to rest.
so that + clause → We moved it so that the night shift could attend.
for + noun (function) → This key is for the side door.
notes: Never write “for + infinitive”: “for to open” and “I came for see you” are both wrong.
Function takes “for + -ing” or “to + verb”: “used for storing data” / “used to store data”. Both are correct.
Use “for + object + infinitive” when the person acting is not the subject of the main clause.
“So that” is the choice when the purpose clause needs a modal — can, could, would — or a different subject.
The negative purpose form is “in order not to”, not “to not”.
grammar.deep: Purpose is the most common thing you will ever need to express in a technical or professional context, and English gives you a scale of forms rather than a single one. A bare “to + verb” is neutral and covers most cases. “In order to” and “so as to” raise the register and are useful in writing, and they are the only forms that comfortably take the negative — “in order not to lose data”. The structure that unlocks real precision is “for + object + infinitive”, because it names whose purpose is being served: “we rescheduled the drill for the new crew to take part” tells you something that “we rescheduled the drill to take part” cannot. When the purpose needs a modal, switch to “so that”, which accepts a full clause: “label the containers so that nobody can mix them up.” Between them, these four forms handle every purpose you will need to express.

chart.title: Expressing purpose
rows: in order to / so as to
We left early in order to avoid delays.
in order not to / so as not to
I wrote so as not to forget.
We waited for the engineer to arrive.
needs a modal or new subject
Move it so that everyone can see.
This valve is for releasing pressure.

examples: The bay was cleared in order to give the technicians room to work.
We printed a second copy for the auditors to take away.
Label every container so that nobody can confuse them.
This panel is for accessing the coolant lines, not for storage.
grammar.watch: Never “for + infinitive”. Purpose is “to do”; function is “for doing”; a different subject takes “for someone to do”.
more: The bay was cleared in order to give the technicians room.
We printed a second copy for the auditors to take away.
Label every container so that nobody can confuse them.
I whispered so as not to wake the crew.
The form is designed to be completed online.
They kept the original for the inspector to check.

fix.wrong: We stopped for refuel.
fix.right: We stopped to refuel.
fix.why: Purpose takes an infinitive, never “for + verb”.

fix.wrong: I left early for not to be late.
fix.right: I left early so as not to be late.
fix.why: The negative purpose forms are “so as not to” and “in order not to”.

fix.wrong: We printed a copy for the auditors take away.
fix.right: We printed a copy for the auditors to take away.
fix.why: A different subject requires “for + person + to + verb”.

drill.name: State the purpose
drill.prompt: Give the purpose of each action three ways: with “to”, with “in order to”, and with “so that + clause”.

dialogue.line: Why keep the original packaging?
For the inspector to check the serial numbers.
Couldn’t we photograph them?
We do that too, so that nothing depends on one record.

contrast.title: Purpose structures
rows: in order to / so as to
in order not to / so as not to

grammar.sound: “So as to” compresses to /ˈsəʊəztə/ and “in order to” to /ɪnˈɔːdətə/; both are single unstressed runs before the stressed verb.

grammar.name: Giving reasons with because, since, because of, for, due to and the reason
grammar.short: because it failed / because of the failure / the reason is that…
grammar.rule: Reason connectors differ in grammar more than in meaning, and the category decides the punctuation. Conjunctions take clauses, prepositions take nouns, and the noun-phrase frames take a that-clause.
form: because + clause → We stopped because the pump failed.
since / as + clause (known reason, often first) → Since nobody replied, I decided myself.
because of / due to / owing to + noun → We stopped due to a pump failure.
as a result of + noun → Two flights were cancelled as a result of the storm.
The reason why … is that … → The reason why we stopped is that the pump failed.
so + clause (result, mirror image) → The pump failed, so we stopped.
notes: “Because of”, “due to” and “owing to” must be followed by a noun or gerund: “due to it failed” is wrong.
“Since” and “as” present the reason as already known and usually come first; “because” carries new information and usually comes second.
Write “the reason is that”, not “the reason is because” — the latter is redundant.
“So” introduces the result, “because” the cause: they are mirror images of the same relationship.
“For” meaning “because” is literary and easily misused at this level; prefer “because” or “since”.
grammar.deep: Cause and result are two views of one relationship, and which half you put in the main clause changes what your reader treats as important, because English weights the second clause more heavily. “The flight was cancelled, so we stayed another night” foregrounds the outcome; “we stayed another night because the flight was cancelled” foregrounds the explanation. Use that deliberately. The mechanical trap is category confusion: if you can see a subject and a verb after the connector, you need “because”, “since” or “as”; if you can see only a noun phrase, you need “because of”, “due to” or “owing to”. The frame “the reason why … is that …” is worth having because it announces that an explanation is coming, which is useful in a long sentence — but keep “is that”, since “the reason is because” says the same thing twice.

chart.title: Reason and result connectors
rows: We stopped because of the failure.
The delay was due to the failure.
It closed as a result of the fault.
The reason we stopped is that it failed.

examples: We rescheduled the test because the pressure readings were unstable.
Owing to a shortage of parts, the refit has been pushed back two weeks.
Since nobody had signed the form, the request was never processed.
The reason why we changed supplier is that the last delivery arrived damaged.
grammar.watch: “Because” + clause, “because of / due to” + noun, and “the reason is that”, never “the reason is because”.
more: We stopped the line because the pump failed.
The launch was postponed due to a fault in the fuel line.
Since nobody replied, I made the decision myself.
The reason we changed supplier is that the old one kept missing deadlines.
Owing to the strike, deliveries were suspended.
It was cancelled because of the weather, not the crew.

fix.wrong: The launch was postponed because a fault in the fuel line.
fix.right: …because of a fault in the fuel line.
fix.why: A noun phrase needs “because of”, not “because”.

fix.wrong: The reason is because it failed.
fix.right: The reason is that it failed.
fix.why: “The reason is” is followed by a that-clause.

fix.wrong: Due to it was raining, we stopped.
fix.right: Because it was raining, we stopped.
fix.why: “Due to” takes a noun; a clause needs a conjunction.

drill.name: Same reason, three forms
drill.prompt: Express each cause three ways: with a conjunction, with a preposition, and with a “the reason … is that” frame.
items: a power cut stopped the shift
a missing signature blocked the order
a software bug lost the data

dialogue.line: Why was the shipment held?
Due to a missing customs form.
Nobody noticed?
The reason it slipped is that two people thought the other had filed it.

grammar.sound: “Because of” reduces to /kəzəv/ in speech, which is why learners hear no difference from “because”. The written form must still be chosen by grammar, not by ear.

speaking.text: Explain the purpose of six objects around you. Use “to + verb” for three and “for + -ing” for three, then add one purpose with “for someone to”.
Defend six decisions you have made, each with a different reason connector. Your partner corrects any category error.
Describe a tool or app you would build: what each feature is for, who it is for, and why the design is as it is.

tips: Purpose = “to do”; function = “for doing”; different subject = “for someone to do”.
“Because” + clause, “due to” + noun.
“The reason is that”, never “the reason is because”.

quiz.q: The launch was postponed ___ a fault in the fuel line.
quiz.explain: “Due to” is a preposition and takes a noun phrase; “because” would require a full clause.

dynamics.name: Manifest audit
dynamics.how: Pairs receive a list of ten items on a manifest and must state, for each, what it is for and why it is there, using a different structure for the two questions.
dynamics.payoff: Separates purpose from reason within one object.

dynamics.name: Because chains
dynamics.how: Groups build a chain of five causes for one event, alternating between conjunctions and prepositions. Any wrong pairing breaks the chain and the group restarts.
dynamics.payoff: The alternation rule is what fixes the because / because of error.

dynamics.name: Instruction rewrite
dynamics.how: Groups take five bare instructions and add a purpose clause to each, then rewrite two with “so that” for a different subject.
dynamics.payoff: Shows why the subject change forces a different structure.

dynamics.name: Formal or neutral
dynamics.how: Teacher reads a sentence; students say which connector fits a report and which fits a conversation, and produce both versions.
dynamics.payoff: Register is where these connectors actually differ.

writing.title: The incident explanation
writing.brief: Explain an incident to a manager. State what was done and why, using at least four purpose structures, and give the causes using at least four different reason connectors, including one formal one.
criteria: Four purpose structures, one negative and one with a different subject.
Four reason connectors, correctly split between clauses and noun phrases.
No “for + infinitive” and no “the reason is because”.

homework.title: Purpose and cause
homework.task: Write eight sentences about decisions you took this week, each with a purpose clause. Then explain the cause of five of them, using a different reason connector each time and marking whether it takes a clause or a noun.

test.q: The launch was postponed ___ a fault in the fuel line.
test.explain: “Due to” is a preposition and takes a noun phrase.

test.q: We stopped ___ .
test.explain: Purpose takes an infinitive.

test.q: We printed a copy ___ take away.
test.explain: A different subject takes “for + person + to + verb”.

test.q: The reason it failed is ___ nobody tested it.
test.explain: “The reason … is” is followed by a that-clause.

test.q: I whispered ___ wake anyone.
test.explain: Negative purpose takes “so as not to” or “in order not to”.

board: Two headings side by side: WHAT FOR? and WHY?
Under WHAT FOR?: to + verb · in order to · so as to · so as not to · for + person + to · for + -ing.
Under WHY?: because + clause · since / as + clause · because of + noun · due to / owing to + noun · the reason … is that.
A vertical line between them labelled PURPOSE (forward) | REASON (backward).
Corner: “the reason is because” crossed out and rewritten with “that”.

units.title: FORENSICS
units.theme: Deducing what happened, and judging what should have happened

overview.intro: Two uses of the same machinery. Past modals let you deduce what happened when you were not there — must have, may have, might have, could have — and then judge the decisions that were taken: should have, could have, would have. One reads the evidence; the other reads the choices.
goals: Express degrees of certainty about the past with must, may, might and could + have.
Use can’t have and couldn’t have for confident negative deductions.
Judge past actions with should have, could have and would have.
overview.outcome: By the end you can analyse an incident at three levels of certainty and deliver a fair judgement on the decisions involved.

vocab.def: facts that show something is true.
vocab.use: Uncountable: “some evidence”, “a piece of evidence”, never “evidences”.
examples: There’s no evidence that anyone tampered with it.
The evidence suggests a software fault.
vocab.colloc: clear evidence · lack of evidence

vocab.def: to accept something as true without checking.
vocab.use: Followed by a that-clause: “I assumed you knew.” Noun: assumption.
examples: I assumed the checks had been done.
Don’t assume anything.
vocab.colloc: safe to assume · a reasonable assumption

vocab.def: to decide that something is not the cause.
vocab.use: Separable: “rule out human error”, “rule it out”.
examples: We can rule out a power failure.
Nothing has been ruled out yet.
vocab.colloc: rule out a cause · can’t rule it out

vocab.def: believable, reasonable as an explanation.
vocab.use: For explanations and accounts: “a plausible theory”. Opposite: implausible.
examples: That’s the most plausible explanation.
His account isn’t plausible.
vocab.colloc: a plausible explanation · perfectly plausible

vocab.def: to fail to notice something.
vocab.use: Transitive. Not the same as “oversee”, which means to supervise.
examples: Somebody must have overlooked the warning.
One detail was overlooked.
vocab.colloc: easily overlooked · overlook an error

vocab.def: failure to take proper care.
vocab.use: Uncountable and quite formal: “gross negligence”. Adjective: negligent.
examples: The report found no negligence.
It was negligence rather than sabotage.
vocab.colloc: gross negligence · through negligence

vocab.def: certain to happen.
vocab.use: “Be bound to + verb”: “It was bound to fail eventually.”
examples: With that load, it was bound to overheat.
She’s bound to notice.
vocab.colloc: bound to happen · bound to fail

vocab.def: probably, as far as one can judge.
vocab.use: Usually at the start of a clause: “Presumably nobody checked.” A hedge for deductions.
examples: Presumably they ran the tests.
He was, presumably, unaware.
vocab.colloc: presumably not · presumably because

vocab.def: to explain or to be the cause of.
vocab.use: Inseparable: “that accounts for the noise”. Also means “to make up a proportion”.
examples: That would account for the pressure drop.
Nothing accounts for the missing hour.
vocab.colloc: account for the difference · unaccounted for

vocab.def: an assumption of innocence when the evidence is unclear.
vocab.use: “Give someone the benefit of the doubt.”
examples: I’d give her the benefit of the doubt.
They gave the crew the benefit of the doubt.
vocab.colloc: give someone the benefit of the doubt

vocab.term: to give someone the benefit of the doubt
vocab.def: to choose the innocent explanation when the evidence is unclear.
vocab.use: Used when a deduction stays tentative: “It might have been an accident — I’d give her the benefit of the doubt.”
examples: I’ll give him the benefit of the doubt this time.
The report gives the crew the benefit of the doubt.
vocab.colloc: give someone the benefit of the doubt

grammar.name: Past modals for degrees of certainty
grammar.short: It must have overheated. It may have been the sensor. It can’t have been sabotage.
grammar.rule: To deduce about the past, add “have + past participle” to a modal of certainty. “Must have” is a confident conclusion, “may / might / could have” leave the question open, and “can’t / couldn’t have” reject a possibility.
form: must have + participle → The seal must have failed.
may / might / could have + participle → It might have been a software error.
may not / might not have + participle → She might not have seen the alert.
can’t / couldn’t have + participle → He can’t have known about it.
Continuous: must have been + -ing → They must have been running diagnostics.
notes: The negative of deductive “must” is “can’t”, never “mustn’t”: “mustn’t” means prohibition.
“May not have” and “might not have” express a real possibility that something is untrue.
“Could have” has two readings: a past possibility (“it could have been the cable”) and an unrealised one (“we could have prevented it”). Context decides.
“Should have” in this family means expectation rather than deduction: “The parts should have arrived by now.”
Adverbs do the same job differently: presumably, evidently, possibly, almost certainly.
grammar.deep: Deduction is a scale and the modals are the marks along it. At the top, “must have” means you have evidence and have drawn a conclusion — it never means you know for certain, which is exactly why it is honest. In the middle, “may”, “might” and “could have” are practically interchangeable, with “may” a little more formal. At the bottom, English does something asymmetrical that catches learners out: the negative conclusion is “can’t have”, not “mustn’t have”, because prohibition has already claimed that form. Keep two ladders separate in your head — one for deduction, one for rules — and remember that the whole structure contracts heavily in speech (“must’ve”, “can’t’ve”), which makes it far harder to hear than to build. Training your ear on these clusters improves your listening as much as your grammar.

chart.title: Certainty about the past
rows: The parts should have arrived by now.
It might have been the sensor.
She might not have seen it.

examples: The pressure dropped overnight, so a seal must have failed somewhere.
It may have been a software fault, but we can’t rule out the wiring.
She can’t have received the alert — her console was offline.
They must have been running the test when the power cut out.
grammar.watch: For a negative deduction use “can’t have”, not “mustn’t have”.
more: The pressure dropped overnight, so a seal must have failed.
It may have been a software error, but we can’t rule out the wiring.
She can’t have received the alert — her console was offline.
Somebody might have moved it during the night shift.
They must have known before the meeting.
It could have been worse if the backup hadn’t started.

fix.wrong: She mustn’t have seen the alert.
fix.right: She can’t have seen the alert.
fix.why: A negative deduction takes “can’t have”, not “mustn’t have”.

fix.wrong: It must have be a fault.
fix.right: It must have been a fault.
fix.why: After “have” the verb takes the past participle.

fix.wrong: Maybe it can have been the sensor.
fix.right: It may have been the sensor.
fix.why: “Can have” is not used for a specific past guess.

drill.name: Read the evidence
drill.prompt: Give three deductions about each situation, at three levels of certainty, and say what evidence supports each.
items: the door was unlocked at seven
two mugs on an empty desk
the log has a two-hour gap

dialogue.line: How did the temperature climb so fast?
A seal must have failed. Nothing else would do that.
Could it have been the sensor?
It can’t have been — the second sensor read the same. It may have started earlier than we think.

contrast.title: Past certainty
rows: She might not have seen it.

grammar.sound: “Must have” becomes /ˈmʌstəv/ and “can’t have” /ˈkɑːntəv/. The modal keeps the stress and “have” disappears into it.

grammar.name: Past modals for judgments and suggestions
grammar.short: They should have checked. We could have prevented it. I would have waited.
grammar.rule: The same structure judges past decisions. “Should have” criticises or regrets, “could have” names a missed possibility or a better option, and “would have” states what you yourself would have done in that situation.
form: should / shouldn’t have + participle → They should have run a second test.
could have + participle → We could have caught it earlier.
couldn’t have + participle → They couldn’t have known at that stage.
would / wouldn’t have + participle → I would have waited another day.
ought to have + participle (more formal) → They ought to have reported it.
notes: Always modal + have + participle: never “should had” and never “should of”.
“Should have” criticises the past; “should” alone advises the present.
“Would have” usually implies a condition, stated or unstated: “I would have waited (if it had been my call).”
“Could have” as judgement is softer than “should have”: it suggests an option rather than an obligation.
“Ought to have” is slightly more formal than “should have” and otherwise identical.
grammar.deep: These forms let you talk about roads not taken, which is why they carry so much social weight. “They should have checked” assigns fault. “They could have checked” points at a missed option without accusing. “I would have checked” makes it about your own judgement rather than their failure — the diplomatic choice when you are reviewing someone else’s work. In a professional post-mortem, moving between the three is what separates a fair review from an attack, and English speakers read the difference immediately. Structurally there is nothing new: the modal never changes, “have” never changes, and only the participle varies. The persistent errors are orthographic rather than grammatical — “should of” for “should’ve” — and the listening challenge is that all three contract into a single unstressed syllable, so the participle is often the only clue to which modal was used.

chart.title: Judging past decisions
rows: We could have run a second test.

examples: The crew should have logged the anomaly instead of resetting the panel.
We could have avoided the whole delay by ordering a spare in advance.
In fairness, they couldn’t have known the sensor was faulty.
I would have grounded the flight, but it wasn’t my decision.
grammar.watch: “Should have”, never “should of” or “should had” — and remember “could have” is softer than “should have”.
more: They should have run a second test before signing off.
We could have caught it earlier if anyone had checked the log.
I would have waited for the supplier’s confirmation.
You shouldn’t have overridden the alarm.
They couldn’t have known — the data only arrived afterwards.
We might have avoided the whole shutdown.

fix.wrong: They should have to check it.
fix.right: They should have checked it.
fix.why: The structure is should + have + past participle, with no “to”.

fix.wrong: We could have caught it if they told us.
fix.right: We could have caught it if they had told us.
fix.why: An unreal past condition takes the past perfect.

fix.wrong: You shouldn’t have not signed it.
fix.right: You should have signed it.
fix.why: Two negatives cancel; state the criticism directly.

drill.name: Judge the decision
drill.prompt: Comment on each decision twice: once with a criticism and once with the alternative you would have chosen.

dialogue.line: Who signed the release?
The night supervisor. He should have waited for the second test.
Would you have signed it?
No. I’d have held it until morning. He couldn’t have known about the sensor, though.

grammar.sound: “Would have” and “could have” reduce to /ˈwʊdəv/ and /ˈkʊdəv/. The difference between them lives in the vowel of the modal, so it must stay distinct.

speaking.text: Given three clues about an unexplained event, produce one deduction with “must have”, two possibilities with “might have”, and one rejection with “can’t have”.
Review a decision that went wrong. Make one “should have”, one “could have”, one “couldn’t have” and one “would have” statement, then decide which was fairest.
One student describes a strange situation from their life. The group speculates using past modals only, until the truth is revealed.

tips: Two ladders: deduction (must / might / can’t have) and judgement (should / could / would have).
The negative deduction is “can’t have”, not “mustn’t have”.
Modal + have + participle, always. Never “should of”.

quiz.q: Her console was offline all night, so she ___ the alert.
quiz.explain: A confident negative deduction about the past takes “can’t have + past participle”.

dynamics.name: Cold case
dynamics.how: Groups receive six pieces of evidence from an incident and must produce a written theory using at least six past modals at different certainty levels, then defend it against another group’s theory.
dynamics.payoff: The challenge round forces precise grading rather than blanket “must have”.

dynamics.name: Can’t have, mustn’t have
dynamics.how: Teacher reads negative deductions, some correct and some using “mustn’t have”; students hold up a card and correct the wrong ones aloud.
dynamics.payoff: Removes the node’s defining error in one focused burst.

dynamics.name: Two-minute inquiry
dynamics.how: A describes a strange situation from real life; B must produce three deductions and one judgement within two minutes, then they swap.
dynamics.payoff: Time pressure prevents rehearsal and exposes what is automatic.

dynamics.name: Hindsight panel
dynamics.how: Groups review three short decisions and issue a verdict on each: what should have happened, what could have happened, what they would have done.
dynamics.payoff: All three judgement modals appear in a single structured output.

writing.title: The forensic report
writing.brief: Reconstruct an incident you know about. Part one: what happened, deduced from the evidence, using at least four past modals at different certainty levels. Part two: a judgement on the decisions taken, using should have, could have and would have.
criteria: Four deductions covering confident, tentative and negative certainty.
Three judgement modals, each doing a different job.
No “mustn’t have” used as a deduction.

homework.title: Evidence and verdict
homework.task: Write six deductions about situations you noticed this week, one at each level of certainty, then six judgements about decisions taken around you, using should have, shouldn’t have, could have and would have.

test.q: Her console was offline all night, so she ___ the alert.
test.explain: A confident negative deduction about the past takes “can’t have”.

test.q: The pressure dropped, so a seal ___ .
test.explain: Must + have + past participle.

test.q: It ___ been a software error, but we’re not sure.
test.explain: An open possibility takes may, might or could.

test.q: They ___ run a second test before signing.
test.explain: Criticism of a past decision takes “should have” + participle.

test.q: We ___ caught it earlier if anyone had checked.
test.explain: A missed past possibility takes “could have” + participle.

Beside it, a red note: MUSTN’T HAVE does not exist as a deduction.
Right half headed JUDGEMENT: should have · shouldn’t have · could have · would have · couldn’t have.
Under both: MODAL + HAVE + PAST PARTICIPLE, written once, large.
Corner pronunciation box: must’ve /ˈmʌstəv/ · could’ve /ˈkʊdəv/ — never “of”.

units.title: ASSEMBLY LINE
units.theme: Describing a process, and adding information precisely

overview.intro: Two structures that carry technical writing. The passive describes a process step by step without naming the workers, and modal passives state what must or should be done. Relative clauses then let you add information, and the comma decides whether that information identifies or merely describes.
goals: Describe a process with is/are + past participle and modal + be + past participle.
Sequence process steps with then, next, after that and once.
Distinguish defining from non-defining relative clauses and punctuate them correctly.
overview.outcome: By the end you can write a six-step process description and add three non-defining clauses to a paragraph without breaking its punctuation.

vocab.def: to put the parts of something together.
vocab.use: Transitive: “assemble the frame”. Noun: assembly. Frequently passive in process descriptions.
examples: The frames are assembled by hand.
Once the unit is assembled, it’s tested.
vocab.colloc: assembly line · assembled by hand

vocab.def: to examine something carefully and officially.
vocab.use: Transitive: “inspect the welds”. Noun: inspection; person: inspector.
examples: Every batch is inspected before shipping.
The welds must be inspected twice.
vocab.colloc: a full inspection · inspected for defects

vocab.def: to separate things into groups.
vocab.use: Transitive: “sort the components by size”. Also “sort out” = resolve.
examples: The beans are sorted by size and colour.
We sorted out the problem in an hour.
vocab.colloc: sort by size · sort out a problem

vocab.def: to get rid of something properly.
vocab.use: Inseparable, always with “of”: “dispose of the waste”. Noun: disposal.
examples: Waste must be disposed of safely.
How is the residue disposed of?
vocab.colloc: dispose of waste · safe disposal

vocab.def: a quantity produced or processed at one time.
vocab.use: Countable: “a batch of components”, “in batches of fifty”.
examples: Each batch is labelled and dated.
We process it in small batches.
vocab.colloc: a batch number · in batches

vocab.def: one part of a longer process.
vocab.use: Countable: “the final stage”, “at this stage”. Slightly more formal than “step”.
examples: At the next stage the parts are coated.
It failed at the testing stage.
vocab.colloc: the final stage · a two-stage process

vocab.def: the basic substance from which something is made.
vocab.use: Usually plural: “raw materials are delivered weekly”.
examples: The raw materials are sourced locally.
Raw material costs have doubled.
vocab.colloc: raw materials · source raw materials

vocab.def: the system for checking standards.
vocab.use: Uncountable, often abbreviated QC: “quality control rejected the batch”.
examples: Quality control is carried out at every stage.
It was flagged by quality control.
vocab.colloc: strict quality control · pass quality control

vocab.def: to have an identifying label attached.
vocab.use: “Each unit is labelled with a serial number.” US spelling: labeled.
examples: Every container is labelled and sealed.
The samples weren’t labelled correctly.
vocab.colloc: clearly labelled · labelled with

vocab.def: showing possession inside a relative clause.
vocab.use: For people and things: “the supplier whose parts failed”. Never write “who’s”.
examples: The technician whose report we read has left.
A machine whose sensors fail is dangerous.
vocab.colloc: whose name · whose fault

vocab.def: to organise something or resolve a problem.
vocab.use: Separable: “sort it out”. Common in process descriptions and in complaints.
examples: The items are sorted out by size before packing.
We sorted the problem out in an hour.
vocab.colloc: sort it out · sort out the details · get it sorted

grammar.name: The passive to describe a process
grammar.short: The parts are cleaned, then they are inspected. Each unit must be tested.
grammar.rule: A process description uses the present passive, because what matters is the sequence of actions rather than who performs them. Modal passives — must be, should be, can be, has to be — state requirements at each stage.
form: Simple present passive: is / are + past participle → The parts are cleaned in three baths.
Modal passive: modal + be + past participle → Every unit must be tested.
Negative: aren’t + participle / mustn’t be + participle → Waste mustn’t be poured away.
Sequencing: First… Then… Next… After that… Once… Finally…
With “by” only when the agent matters: The samples are checked by an external lab.
notes: The agent is almost never mentioned in a process description — the sequence is the point.
Keep the subject constant where possible, so the reader follows one thing through the chain.
Adverbs of frequency go between “be” and the participle: “Filters are usually replaced monthly.”
Modal passives are the standard form for rules and requirements: “Helmets must be worn”, “Forms should be signed”.
Do not mix “being” into a simple present passive: “is cleaned”, not “is being cleaned”, unless you really mean right now.
grammar.deep: Process writing is where the passive stops being a grammar exercise and becomes the obvious choice. Each step keeps the product as its subject — “the beans are picked, washed, dried and sorted” — so the reader tracks one thing through a chain of actions instead of following a cast of workers. That cohesion is the whole point, and it is why manuals, standards and procedure documents are written almost entirely in this form. Modal passives extend it to requirements, which is why every notice you have ever read is built the same way: “tickets must be shown”, “containers should be sealed”. Two practical habits: keep the subject constant so the sequence reads smoothly, and add explicit sequencing words at the joints, because a passive chain without signposts is hard to follow even when every sentence is correct.

chart.title: Process and requirement forms
rows: The filter should be checked weekly.
Samples may be stored for a week.

examples: First the components are degreased, then they are dried and inspected.
Every batch must be labelled with a date and a serial number before it is stored.
Once the unit has been assembled, it can be tested at low pressure.
Residue mustn’t be disposed of through the normal drains.
grammar.watch: “Is cleaned” for a routine step; “is being cleaned” only for something happening right now.
more: First the components are degreased, then they are dried and inspected.
Every batch must be labelled with a date before it is stored.
The parts are cleaned in three baths and left overnight.
Once the unit has been assembled, it is tested twice.
Damaged items are set aside and are not returned to the line.
Each container should be weighed before it leaves the bay.

fix.wrong: The parts are being cleaned in three baths every morning.
fix.right: The parts are cleaned in three baths every morning.
fix.why: A routine step takes the simple passive; the continuous is only for right now.

fix.wrong: Every unit must be test.
fix.right: Every unit must be tested.
fix.why: A modal passive is modal + be + past participle.

fix.wrong: The batch is label with a date.
fix.right: The batch is labelled with a date.
fix.why: The participle must carry the -ed.

drill.name: Six steps
drill.prompt: Describe each process in six passive steps with no named agent, using at least one modal passive.
items: how a room is prepared for an exam

dialogue.line: What happens after assembly?
The unit is tested, then it’s labelled and logged.
And if it fails?
It’s pulled from the line. The whole batch has to be re-inspected before anything is released.

contrast.title: Passive choices in a process
rows: It can be cleaned on site.

grammar.sound: In a process description the sequence words carry the stress — FIRST, THEN, ONCE — and the passive verbs run flat behind them. Even stress makes the list impossible to follow.

grammar.name: Defining and non-defining relative clauses
grammar.short: the engineer who signed it · Ana, who signed it,
grammar.rule: A defining clause identifies which person or thing you mean and takes no commas. A non-defining clause adds extra information about something already identified, sits between commas, and cannot use “that”.
form: Defining: The engineer who signed the report has left.
Non-defining: Ana Ruiz, who signed the report, has left.
Things: the machine that failed / the machine, which is ten years old,
Possession: the supplier whose parts failed.
Sentence-modifying which: The test failed twice, which delayed the launch.
notes: “That” is impossible in a non-defining clause: use “who” or “which”.
The pronoun of a non-defining clause can never be omitted.
Commas change the facts: “my brother who lives abroad” implies several brothers; “my brother, who lives abroad,” implies one.
“Which” can refer to the whole preceding clause when it adds a comment: “…, which surprised everyone.”
In speech, a non-defining clause is marked by a pause and a change in intonation where the commas would be.
grammar.deep: The comma is the whole grammar of this topic. A defining clause is part of the identification, so removing it changes who or what you are talking about; a non-defining clause is a parenthesis, so removing it leaves the sentence intact. Two mechanical consequences follow: “that” is banned from non-defining clauses, and the pronoun can never be dropped there, because the commas have already suspended the main clause and something has to hold the parenthesis together. The consequence for meaning is bigger than most learners expect. “The passengers who had boarded early were moved” says only some passengers were moved; “the passengers, who had boarded early, were moved” says all of them were. In technical and legal writing that difference is not stylistic — it is the sentence’s content, which is why punctuation here deserves real attention.

chart.title: Defining vs non-defining
rows: The unit that failed was old.
The unit, which was old, failed.

examples: The technician who ran the second test found the fault immediately.
Our main supplier, which has been with us for a decade, missed two deliveries.
The batch that failed inspection was returned; the rest were shipped.
The launch was delayed twice, which cost us the whole quarter.
grammar.watch: No “that” in a non-defining clause, and never drop the pronoun when there are commas.
more: The engineer who signed the report has left the company.
Ana Ruiz, who signed the report, has left the company.
The machine that failed is ten years old.
The main pump, which was replaced last year, failed again.
The supplier whose invoice was wrong has apologised.
The bay where the accident happened is closed.

fix.why: A non-defining clause about an already identified person needs commas.

units.title: BRIEFING
units.theme: Recommending impersonally, and checking your listener agrees

overview.intro: Two structures for stating a position. Passive modals make a recommendation sound like a general truth rather than your personal instruction, and tag questions turn a statement into an invitation to agree — the most characteristically English move in conversation.
goals: Give recommendations with passive modals: should be, ought to be, must be, has to be, has got to be.
Choose the right strength of passive modal for the situation.
Form tag questions accurately and use intonation to change their function.
overview.outcome: By the end you can deliver a short set of recommendations in impersonal register and hold a five-turn opinion exchange using tags.

vocab.def: advice about what should be done.
vocab.use: Countable: “make a recommendation”, “our recommendations are…”. Verb: recommend.
examples: The report makes four recommendations.
My recommendation is to wait.
vocab.colloc: make a recommendation · strong recommendation

vocab.def: something that must be dealt with first.
vocab.use: Countable: “the top priority”, “set priorities”. “Give priority to + noun”.
examples: Safety has to be the priority.
We need to set clearer priorities.
vocab.colloc: top priority · give priority to

vocab.def: to deal with an issue directly.
vocab.use: Transitive: “address the delay”. Common in formal recommendations.
examples: This has to be addressed before the launch.
The report addresses three issues.
vocab.colloc: address a problem · properly addressed

vocab.def: needing immediate attention.
vocab.use: For situations, not people: “an urgent repair”. Adverb: urgently.
examples: This is urgent — it must be done today.
The panel needs replacing urgently.
vocab.colloc: an urgent matter · a sense of urgency

vocab.def: an informal, emphatic “must”.
vocab.use: “It’s got to be checked.” Common in speech, rare in formal writing.
examples: That’s got to be fixed before Monday.
This has got to stop.
vocab.colloc: has got to be · you’ve got to

vocab.def: should — slightly more formal.
vocab.use: Always with “to”: “It ought to be reviewed.” Negative: “ought not to”.
examples: The manual ought to be updated.
They ought to have told us.
vocab.colloc: ought to be · ought not to

vocab.def: to remember and consider something.
vocab.use: “Bear in mind that…” or “bear it in mind”. Note the spelling: bear, not bare.
examples: Bear in mind that the parts take a week.
It should be borne in mind that costs vary.
vocab.colloc: bear in mind that · worth bearing in mind

vocab.def: possible and practical to do.
vocab.use: For plans: “a feasible timeline”. Noun: feasibility.
examples: That isn’t feasible in two weeks.
Is it feasible to run both systems?
vocab.colloc: technically feasible · a feasible option

vocab.def: to investigate.
vocab.use: Inseparable: “this should be looked into”. Very common as a passive recommendation.
examples: The complaint should be looked into.
We’ll look into it this week.
vocab.colloc: look into a matter · worth looking into

vocab.def: used to invite agreement about something you consider obvious.
vocab.use: Not the same as “certainly”: “Surely that’s not right?” expresses surprise and expects agreement.
examples: Surely they must have noticed?
That surely can’t be the final figure.
vocab.colloc: surely not · surely you agree

vocab.def: to raise a subject for discussion.
vocab.use: Separable: “bring it up”. The natural verb for the briefing genre.
examples: I’ll bring it up at the next meeting.
Nobody brought up the cost.
vocab.colloc: bring up a point · bring it up · worth bringing up

grammar.name: Recommendations and opinions with passive modals
grammar.short: It should be reviewed. This has to be dealt with today.
grammar.rule: A passive modal states what needs to happen without naming who must do it. The structure is modal + be + past participle, and the choice of modal grades the strength from a suggestion to a requirement.
form: should be / ought to be + participle → The manual should be updated.
must be / has to be + participle → All entries must be signed.
has got to be + participle (informal, emphatic) → This has got to be fixed.
could be / might be + participle (tentative) → The layout could be simplified.
Negative: shouldn’t be / mustn’t be + participle → Passwords mustn’t be shared.
notes: “Should be” and “ought to be” are recommendations; “must be” and “has to be” are requirements.
“Has got to be” is emphatic and informal — natural in speech, out of place in a written report.
The passive removes the agent, which is what makes the recommendation sound objective rather than personal.
Add “by” only when the responsible party matters: “This must be approved by the safety officer.”
“Must be” also means deduction in other contexts (“she must be tired”), so make the recommendation clear from the context.
grammar.deep: There is a real difference between “you should update the manual” and “the manual should be updated”. The first is your instruction to a person; the second is a statement about the world, and it lands as an assessment rather than an order. That is why passive modals dominate reports, audits and reviews: they let you be firm about the action while staying neutral about the actor. The grading is what makes them useful. “Could be” floats an option, “should be” recommends, “has to be” states a requirement, and “has got to be” adds emotional pressure that belongs only in speech. Two mechanics keep them clean: the modal never changes form, so all the work is done by “be” plus the participle, and the negatives shift meaning rather than fading — “shouldn’t be shared” is advice, “mustn’t be shared” is a prohibition.

chart.title: Strength of passive modals
rows: The policy ought to be reviewed.
Every entry has to be signed.
Waste must be disposed of safely.
This has got to be sorted out.

examples: The checklist should be revised before the next inspection.
All maintenance records have to be signed by a supervisor.
This has got to be dealt with today — we can’t run another shift like that.
Access codes mustn’t be shared, and they ought to be changed monthly.
grammar.watch: Modal + be + past participle: “should be updated”, never “should updated” or “should be update”.
more: The checklist should be revised before the next inspection.
All maintenance records have to be signed by a supervisor.
This has got to be dealt with today.
Nothing ought to be released without a second signature.
The figures must be checked against the original file.
These forms can be submitted electronically now.

fix.right: The manual should be updated.
fix.why: A passive modal always keeps “be”.

fix.wrong: It should be update before Friday.
fix.right: It should be updated before Friday.
fix.why: The verb after “be” must be a past participle.

fix.wrong: The records have to signed by a supervisor.
fix.right: The records have to be signed by a supervisor.
fix.why: “Have to” also requires “be” in the passive.

drill.prompt: Turn each personal instruction into an impersonal recommendation with a passive modal, then grade it up or down in strength.
items: you should back up the file
we have to review the checklist
you can send it by email
somebody ought to update the manual

contrast.title: Strength of a passive modal
rows: It’s got to be done today.

grammar.name: Tag questions for opinions
grammar.short: That’s the real problem, isn’t it?
grammar.rule: A tag question turns a statement into a check. Repeat the auxiliary, reverse the polarity, and use a pronoun. Positive statements take negative tags and negative statements take positive tags.
form: Positive statement, negative tag: You’ve seen the report, haven’t you?
Negative statement, positive tag: You haven’t seen it, have you?
No auxiliary → use do: She works upstairs, doesn’t she?
With modals: It should be replaced, shouldn’t it?
Irregular: I’m late, aren’t I? · Let’s start, shall we? · Nobody called, did they?
notes: Intonation changes the function: falling intonation asks for agreement, rising intonation asks a genuine question.
The tag repeats the auxiliary of the statement: “I’ve finished, haven’t I?”, “She left, didn’t she?”.
Indefinite subjects take “they” in the tag: “Nobody noticed, did they?”, “Everyone agreed, didn’t they?”
Imperatives take “will you” or “would you”: “Close the door, will you?”
“I am” has the irregular tag “aren’t I?”, not “amn’t I”.
grammar.deep: Tags are what make English conversation feel collaborative. Instead of asserting a view and waiting, a speaker states it and immediately invites the other person in — “that was the real problem, wasn’t it?” — which converts a monologue into an exchange. The grammar is mechanical and can be automated with practice: find the auxiliary, flip the polarity, add the pronoun. What learners underestimate is intonation, because it carries the whole function. Falling intonation means you expect agreement and are really seeking confirmation; rising intonation means you genuinely do not know. Use the wrong one and you either sound as though you are interrogating a colleague or as though you have already decided their answer. Learn the irregular handful — “aren’t I”, “shall we”, “will you”, “did they” after nobody — and the rest follows from the auxiliary.
examples: That’s the real bottleneck, isn’t it?
You haven’t signed the log yet, have you?
This ought to be reviewed before Friday, oughtn’t it?
Nobody actually tested it under load, did they?
grammar.watch: The tag repeats the statement’s auxiliary and reverses the polarity: “I’m right, aren’t I?”, never “amn’t I”.
more: That’s the real problem, isn’t it?
You’ve seen the report, haven’t you?
You haven’t signed it yet, have you?
She works upstairs, doesn’t she?
There’s no easy answer, is there?
Let’s leave it there, shall we?

fix.wrong: You’ve seen it, isn’t it?
fix.right: You’ve seen it, haven’t you?
fix.why: The tag repeats the auxiliary of the statement.

fix.wrong: She works upstairs, doesn’t her?
fix.right: She works upstairs, doesn’t she?
fix.why: The tag takes a subject pronoun.

fix.wrong: I’m late, amn’t I?
fix.right: I’m late, aren’t I?
fix.why: “Aren’t I” is the fixed English form.

drill.prompt: Add the correct tag to each statement, then say it twice: once falling, as a check, and once rising, as a genuine question.

grammar.sound: A falling tag is a check that expects agreement; a rising tag is a real question. Same words, opposite meaning, so the intonation must be deliberate.

Grade the strength deliberately: could be, should be, has to be.
The tag repeats the auxiliary; intonation decides whether it is a check or a question.

units.title: LOGBOOK
units.theme: What you have achieved, and what you intend to achieve

overview.intro: The last sector closes the log. First, accomplishments: the simple past for finished achievements and the present perfect for what you have done in a period that is still open. Then goals: the future perfect for what you will have completed, and “would like to have + participle” for the ambitions you hope to look back on.
goals: Talk about accomplishments with the simple past and the present perfect.
Set goals with the future perfect.
Express hoped-for achievements with would like to have + past participle.
overview.outcome: By the end you can present your achievements in a two-minute personal statement and set three dated goals in precise future forms.

vocab.def: something impressive that you have achieved.
vocab.use: Countable: “a major accomplishment”. Verb: accomplish. British English often prefers “achievement”.
examples: Finishing the course was a real accomplishment.
Her accomplishments speak for themselves.
vocab.colloc: a major accomplishment · a sense of accomplishment

vocab.def: to succeed in doing something after effort.
vocab.use: Takes goals and results, not objects: “achieve a target”, not “achieve a car”.
examples: We achieved everything we planned.
She has achieved a lot in two years.
vocab.colloc: achieve a goal · achieve success

vocab.def: to decide on something you want to achieve.
vocab.use: “Set a goal”, not “put a goal”. “Reach” or “meet” a goal when you succeed.
examples: I set myself three goals for this year.
We met every goal except one.
vocab.colloc: set a goal · reach a goal · realistic goals

vocab.def: up to now, in a period still open.
vocab.use: A present perfect signal, usually at the end: “I’ve completed four modules so far.”
examples: So far I’ve visited eleven countries.
Nothing has gone wrong so far.
vocab.colloc: so far so good · so far this year

vocab.def: to gain the official right to do a job.
vocab.use: “Qualify as + profession” or “qualify for + noun”: “qualify as an engineer”.
examples: She qualified as a paramedic last year.
I don’t qualify for the grant.
vocab.colloc: qualify as · newly qualified

vocab.def: an important point in a plan or a life.
vocab.use: Countable: “reach a milestone”, “a major milestone”.
examples: Publishing it was a milestone for the team.
The next milestone is certification.
vocab.colloc: reach a milestone · a major milestone

vocab.def: to think about something in your past.
vocab.use: Three parts: “look back on my twenties”. Pairs naturally with “would like to have”.
examples: I’d like to look back on this as a turning point.
She looks back on it fondly.
vocab.colloc: look back on it · looking back

vocab.def: over a long period in the future.
vocab.use: Usually at the start or end: “In the long run, it will save money.”
examples: In the long run, the investment pays off.
It’s cheaper in the long run.
vocab.colloc: in the long run · in the short term

vocab.def: to fail to reach a standard or target.
vocab.use: “Fall short of expectations / the target”.
examples: We fell short of the target by two per cent.
It fell short of what we expected.
vocab.colloc: fall short of the target

vocab.def: sensible and possible in practice.
vocab.use: For goals and plans: “a realistic timeline”. Opposite: unrealistic.
examples: Is that a realistic goal for six months?
Be realistic about how long it takes.
vocab.colloc: a realistic target · perfectly realistic

vocab.def: to feel pleased about something that is going to happen.
vocab.use: Always followed by a noun or -ing, never an infinitive: “I’m looking forward to starting.”
examples: I’m looking forward to finishing the certification.
She’s looking forward to the handover.
vocab.colloc: look forward to it · really looking forward to

grammar.name: Accomplishments with the simple past and present perfect
grammar.short: I finished the course in May. / I’ve completed four modules so far.
grammar.rule: The simple past reports an achievement inside a finished period of time. The present perfect reports it inside a period that is still open, or with no time reference at all when only the result matters.
form: Simple past + finished time → I qualified in 2021. / I finished it last month.
Present perfect + open period → I’ve completed three projects this year.
Present perfect, no time → I’ve worked in four countries.
With for and since → I’ve worked here for six years / since 2019.
Experience question then detail: Have you ever led a team? — Yes, I led one in 2022.
notes: Once you name a finished time, the present perfect is impossible: “I have qualified in 2021” is wrong.
Open-period markers pull the perfect: today, this week, this year, so far, in my career, ever, never, already, yet.
In interviews and personal statements the pattern is perfect first, past second: claim the experience, then date it.
“For” + duration and “since” + starting point both need the present perfect when the situation continues.
Counted results take the perfect in an open period: “I’ve delivered eight sessions this term.”
grammar.deep: Stop asking when it happened and ask whether the box is closed. The simple past puts an achievement in a closed box — last year, in 2021, during my degree — and boxes like that cannot receive anything else. The present perfect puts it in a box that is still on the table: this year, in my career, so far. That is why “I’ve completed three modules this term” makes sense and “I’ve completed three modules last term” does not. In practice the two work as a team, and the sequence matters professionally: open with the perfect to establish that you have the experience, then switch to the past to give the specifics. “I’ve managed remote teams. I led a team of six in 2022” is exactly the rhythm an interviewer expects, and reversing it makes a strong record sound like an anecdote.

chart.title: Which tense for an achievement?
rows: I’ve run four workshops this year.
Have you ever managed a budget?

examples: I’ve led three projects so far this year, and the first one finished ahead of schedule.
She qualified as an engineer in 2019 and has worked in maintenance ever since.
Have you ever presented to a board? — Yes, I did it twice last spring.
We haven’t missed a deadline this quarter, though we missed two last year.
grammar.watch: Never combine finished time with the present perfect: “I finished it last month”, not “I have finished it last month”.
more: I’ve led three projects so far this year.
She qualified as an engineer in 2019 and has worked here ever since.
Have you ever managed a team of more than ten?
We finished the migration last month, ahead of schedule.
I haven’t taken a full week off since March.
He completed the course in June and started here in July.

fix.right: I finished it last month.
fix.why: Finished time takes the simple past.

fix.wrong: I work here since 2019.
fix.right: I’ve worked here since 2019.
fix.why: A period reaching to now takes the present perfect.

fix.wrong: Did you ever manage a team?
fix.right: Have you ever managed a team?
fix.why: “Ever” about life experience takes the present perfect.

drill.name: Open or closed
drill.prompt: Describe each achievement twice: once inside a finished period and once inside a period that is still open.

dialogue.line: What have you done since you joined?
I’ve led three projects and I’ve rebuilt the reporting system.
When did the last one finish?
In March. It ran six weeks over, but nothing has slipped since then.

contrast.title: Simple past or present perfect
rows: this year, so far, this week
Have you ever led a team?
I’ve been here for two years.
I worked there for two years.

grammar.sound: “Have” is unstressed and contracts onto the subject; the participle carries the meaning. “I’ve LED three projects” — stressing “have” signals contradiction.

grammar.name: Goals with the future perfect and would like to have + past participle
grammar.short: By June I’ll have finished. / I’d like to have travelled more by then.
grammar.rule: The future perfect states what will be complete before a future point. “Would like to have + past participle” expresses a hoped-for achievement — what you want to be able to look back on — and is softer and less certain than the future perfect.
form: will have + past participle → By December I’ll have completed the certification.
will have been + -ing (duration) → By May I’ll have been studying for two years.
would like to have + participle → I’d like to have published something by thirty.
would like to be + -ing → In five years I’d like to be running my own team.
hope to have + participle → I hope to have finished by then.
notes: The future perfect needs a future reference point: by then, by June, by the time I’m thirty.
After “by the time”, the verb stays in the present: “By the time I’m thirty, I’ll have finished.”
“Would like to have + participle” is about desire, not prediction — it does not claim the goal will be met.
“I’d like to have finished” and “I’d like to finish” differ: the first looks back from a future point, the second looks forward from now.
State verbs stay simple: “I’ll have known her ten years”, not “will have been knowing”.
grammar.deep: These two forms let you talk about the future from two different vantage points. The future perfect stands at a future date and looks back at completed work — “by the end of the year we’ll have replaced every unit” — which is why it is the language of plans, targets and project reporting. “Would like to have + participle” stands at the same future date but reports a wish rather than a projection: “I’d like to have moved into research by then.” The difference is confidence, and choosing correctly matters in an interview or a review, because the future perfect commits you and the “would like” form does not. Note the recurring rule one last time: after “by the time”, the verb stays in the present, because English marks the future only once, in the main clause. That single principle has run through half of this level.

chart.title: Talking about future achievements
rows: By June I’ll have finished the course.
By May I’ll have been working here a year.
I hope to have qualified by then.
I’d like to have travelled more by thirty.
I’d like to be leading a team in five years.

examples: By the end of next year I’ll have completed both certifications.
By the time the refit finishes, we’ll have been working on it for eight months.
I’d like to have moved into project management by the time I’m thirty.
In five years I’d like to be running my own maintenance team, and I hope to have trained a few people by then.
grammar.watch: After “by the time” the verb stays in the present, and “would like to have + participle” expresses a wish, not a prediction.
more: By December I’ll have completed the certification.
By May I’ll have been studying for two years.
I’d like to have travelled more by the time I’m forty.
We’ll have opened two more sites by the end of next year.
She’d like to have finished the draft before the review.
By then the whole team will have moved to the new system.

fix.wrong: By December I will complete the certification.
fix.right: By December I’ll have completed the certification.
fix.why: Completion before a future point takes the future perfect.

fix.wrong: I’d like to have travel more.
fix.right: I’d like to have travelled more.
fix.why: The structure takes a past participle.

fix.wrong: By the time I will be forty, I’ll have finished.
fix.right: By the time I’m forty, I’ll have finished.
fix.why: A time clause takes no future form.

drill.name: By then
drill.prompt: Set a deadline for each goal and state it twice: with the future perfect, and with “I’d like to have + participle”.

dialogue.line: Where do you want to be in two years?
By then I’ll have finished the certification.
And beyond that?
I’d like to have led a project abroad by the time I’m thirty-five. That’s realistic, I think.

contrast.title: Stating a goal
rows: I’ll have been studying two years.
I’d like to have travelled more.
I plan to apply in March.

grammar.sound: “Will have been” collapses to /ləvbɪn/ after the pronoun, so the whole three-word auxiliary rides on one unstressed beat before the -ing verb.

speaking.text: Present your achievements in two minutes. Open each claim in the present perfect and follow it with a dated detail in the simple past.
Set three dated goals using the future perfect, then restate each one with “would like to have”. Discuss which version feels more honest.
Interview your partner about their record and their plans. Every question must use one of this sector’s structures.

tips: Closed time takes the past; open time takes the perfect.
Claim the experience in the perfect, then date it in the past.
After “by the time”, stay in the present.

quiz.q: By the time the refit is over, we ___ on it for eight months.
quiz.explain: Duration up to a future point takes the future perfect continuous, and “by the time” keeps its own clause in the present.

dynamics.name: Achievement wall
dynamics.how: Students post three achievements without dates. Others circulate asking when each happened, and the owner must answer in the tense the question requires.
dynamics.payoff: The question forces the choice between the two tenses live.

dynamics.name: Two-year plan
dynamics.how: Each student sets three goals with deadlines; the partner interviews them and reports back to the class using the future perfect.
dynamics.payoff: Reporting adds a second pass through the structure.

dynamics.name: Since or in
dynamics.how: Teacher calls time expressions; students respond with a full sentence in the matching tense. Any mismatch is rewritten on the board.
dynamics.payoff: Isolates the signal-to-tense mapping.

dynamics.name: Logbook closing
dynamics.how: Groups write a closing entry for the course: what they have achieved, what they finished and when, and what they will have achieved a year from now.
dynamics.payoff: Closes the level with all three structures in one authentic text.

writing.title: The logbook entry
writing.brief: Write a closing entry on a year of work or study. Part one: what you have achieved and what you finished at specific times. Part two: what you will have achieved by a date you set, and what you would like to have done by then.
criteria: Four present perfects with open time periods and three simple pasts with finished time.
Two future perfects tied to a named deadline.
One “would like to have + past participle”.

homework.title: Then and by then
homework.task: Write eight sentences about what you have achieved this year and what you achieved in specific past months, marking the signal word in each. Then write six goals with deadlines using the future perfect.

test.q: I ___ three projects so far this year.
test.explain: “So far this year” is an open period.

test.q: She ___ as an engineer in 2019.
test.explain: A named finished year takes the simple past.

test.q: By December I ___ the certification.
test.explain: Completion before a deadline takes the future perfect.

test.q: I’d like ___ more by the time I’m forty.
test.explain: The structure is would like to have + past participle.

test.q: By the time I ___ forty, I’ll have finished.
test.explain: A time clause never takes a future form.

board: A single timeline with three zones: FINISHED PERIOD (simple past) · OPEN PERIOD (present perfect) · FUTURE DEADLINE (future perfect).
Under each zone, its signal words: last month, in 2019, yesterday | this year, so far, since, ever | by June, by then, by the time.
A red strike through “I have finished it last month”.
Lower strip: WILL HAVE + participle, and beneath it WOULD LIKE TO HAVE + participle.
Corner: no WILL after by the time.
